posts.post_title: Which type of cell injury is produced by her…
posts.post_content: Which type of cell injury is produced by herpes virus, picornavirus and parvovirus?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Cytocidal effect causing cell death

Herpes virus, picornavirus and parvovirus cause the cytocidal effect, leading to cell death.

Correct Option Explanation

Their capsid proteins are toxic and block host protein, DNA and RNA synthesis, causing necrosis of the infected cell.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Non-cytocidal persistent infection is wrong — arenavirus and retrovirus replicate and bud without killing the cell.
  • Cell transformation is wrong — this non-cytocidal change is caused by oncogenic viruses like polyomavirus and papillomavirus.
  • Latent infection is wrong — here viral genome persists with no replication, as with herpes virus reactivation.
Know More
  • Chronic infection results in infectious carriers, e.g. FMD.
  • Slow viral infection is caused by lentivirus with a long incubation period.
  • Inclusion bodies of canine distemper and measles are both intranuclear and intracytoplasmic.
  • Syncytia formation is typical of herpes and paramyxo viruses.

posts.post_title: Foot and Mouth Disease is caused by a virus…
posts.post_content: Foot and Mouth Disease is caused by a virus of which group?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Picorna virus

Foot and Mouth Disease (FMD) is caused by the Picorna virus group, genus Aphthovirus.

Correct Option Explanation

Prevalent serotypes in India are O, A, C and Asia 1; the disease produces vesicles on the mouth and feet of cloven-footed animals.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Rhabdo virus is wrong — this causes Vesicular stomatitis, a differential diagnosis of FMD.
  • Toga virus is wrong — this causes Equine viral arteritis, not FMD.
  • Reo virus is wrong — Orbivirus of the Reoviridae family causes Bluetongue.
Know More
  • FMD produces the classic 'Tigroid heart' from myocardial degeneration in calves.
  • Diagnosis uses complement fixation test and PCR.
  • FMD sequelae include infertility from thyroid endocrine damage.
  • The disease is rarely fatal except in very young animals.

posts.post_title: Rinderpest is caused by which virus?
posts.post_content: Rinderpest is caused by which virus?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Morbillivirus

Rinderpest, also called cattle plague, is caused by a Morbillivirus.

Correct Option Explanation

This virus is antigenically related to canine distemper, PPR and measles viruses.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Pestivirus is wrong — this causes Bovine Viral Diarrhoea/Mucosal disease.
  • Orbivirus is wrong — this causes Bluetongue and African Horse Sickness.
  • Lentivirus is wrong — this causes diseases like Equine Infectious Anaemia and Visna-Maedi.
Know More
  • Rinderpest produces pathognomonic 'Zebra marking' haemorrhages on rectal mucosal folds.
  • It has not been reported in the Indian subcontinent since June 1995.
  • The disease led to the first veterinary college in 1762 at Lyons, France.
  • Diagnosis differentiates rinderpest from PPR using specific cDNA probes.

posts.post_title: Malignant Catarrhal Fever in cattle is cause…
posts.post_content: Malignant Catarrhal Fever in cattle is caused by which virus?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Gamma-Herpes virus

Malignant Catarrhal Fever (MCF) is caused by a lymphotrophic Gamma-Herpes virus.

Correct Option Explanation

In Africa the wildebeest carries the virus for cattle, while in the US sheep act as the reservoir; it is not transmitted between infected cattle.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Beta-Herpes virus is wrong — MCF is caused specifically by the gamma subgroup, not beta.
  • Adenovirus is wrong — this causes Infectious Canine Hepatitis, not MCF.
  • Parvovirus is wrong — this causes diseases such as Canine Parvoviral Infection and Feline Panleucopenia.
Know More
  • MCF causes a 'cooked-up' appearance of the brain.
  • No inclusion bodies or syncytia are seen in MCF brain lesions.
  • Diagnosis uses ELISA and serum neutralization test.
  • MCF is differentiated from Rinderpest by prominent intestinal lesions.

posts.post_title: The pathognomonic gross lesion of Blue Tongu…
posts.post_content: The pathognomonic gross lesion of Blue Tongue disease in sheep is haemorrhage at which site?

_aimcq_options.text: Base of the pulmonary artery and aorta

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Base of the pulmonary artery and aorta

The pathognomonic lesion of Blue Tongue is haemorrhage at the base of the pulmonary artery and aorta.

Correct Option Explanation

Blue Tongue is caused by an arthropod-borne Orbivirus transmitted by Culicoides midges, producing vascular damage.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Bowman's space haemorrhage is wrong — this microscopic finding is described in Swine Fever.
  • Peyer's patches ulceration is wrong — this is a feature of Rinderpest and PPR, not Blue Tongue.
  • Endocardium lesion is wrong — Blue Tongue haemorrhages are described at the great-vessel base, not the endocardium specifically.
Know More
  • Blue Tongue was first recognised in South Africa in 1902.
  • It can be transmitted via semen from an infected bull.
  • Coronet haemorrhage in Blue Tongue is described as the 'flushing of feet'.
  • It belongs to family Reoviridae.

posts.post_title: Bovine Viral Diarrhoea and Mucosal Disease a…
posts.post_content: Bovine Viral Diarrhoea and Mucosal Disease are caused by which type of virus?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Pestivirus

Both BVD and Mucosal disease are caused by antigenically related pestiviruses.

Correct Option Explanation

Two biotypes exist — cytopathogenic and non-cytopathogenic — and infection can pass transplacentally to the foetus.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Morbillivirus is wrong — this causes Rinderpest and PPR, not BVD.
  • Lentivirus is wrong — this causes slow viral diseases like Visna-Maedi.
  • Parapoxvirus is wrong — this causes Orf and Bovine Papular Stomatitis.
Know More
  • BVD was first reported in New York state in 1946.
  • Congenital cerebellar hypoplasia occurs in calves born to infected dams.
  • Cross serum neutralization test differentiates BVD from Rinderpest.
  • Persistently infected calves remain viraemic for life.

posts.post_title: Infectious Bovine Rhinotracheitis (IBRT) is…
posts.post_content: Infectious Bovine Rhinotracheitis (IBRT) is caused by which agent?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Bovine herpes virus type 1

IBRT is caused by Bovine herpes virus type 1 (BHV-1).

Correct Option Explanation

The virus survives up to one year in frozen semen and can spread through the trigeminal nerve to cause non-suppurative encephalitis.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • BHV-4 is wrong — BHV-1, not BHV-4, is the accepted causative agent of IBRT.
  • Bovine adenovirus is wrong — this is only implicated as a contributor to Shipping Fever.
  • Parainfluenza-3 is wrong — this is also a Shipping Fever contributor, not the IBRT agent.
Know More
  • IBRT is also called infectious pustular vulvovaginitis.
  • Genital form clinical signs appear 24–72 hours after coitus with an infected bull.
  • Up to 60% of pregnant cows in a herd may abort.
  • Diagnosis uses ELISA, IFT, IPT and electron microscopy.

posts.post_title: Peste-des-Petits-Ruminants (PPR) is caused b…
posts.post_content: Peste-des-Petits-Ruminants (PPR) is caused by which virus?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Morbillivirus

PPR, or goat plague, is caused by a Morbillivirus.

Correct Option Explanation

PPR was first reported in Africa in 1942, and in India in 1989 in Villupuram district, Tamil Nadu.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Orbivirus is wrong — this causes Bluetongue, not PPR.
  • Pestivirus is wrong — this causes BVD/Mucosal disease.
  • Lentivirus is wrong — this causes slow viral diseases such as Maedi-Visna and CAE.
Know More
  • PPR produces 'Zebra stripes' in the ileo-caecal junction like Rinderpest.
  • Unlike Rinderpest, PPR shows pneumonia as a differentiating feature.
  • Disease is more severe in goats than sheep.
  • Diagnosis uses AGID, immuno-capture ELISA and RT-PCR.

posts.post_title: Equine Infectious Anaemia is caused by which…
posts.post_content: Equine Infectious Anaemia is caused by which type of virus?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Lentivirus

Equine Infectious Anaemia (EIA) is caused by a Lentivirus.

Correct Option Explanation

The virus shares serological reactivity with the human AIDS lentivirus and persists in blood throughout the horse's life.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Morbillivirus is wrong — this causes cattle and small ruminant diseases such as Rinderpest and PPR.
  • Orbivirus is wrong — this causes African Horse Sickness, a different equine viral disease.
  • Arenavirus is wrong — this is only cited as an example of persistent, non-cytocidal infection.
Know More
  • EIA was first recorded in India in 1987 at a stud farm in Bangalore.
  • The Coggins test (AGID), developed in 1972, detects antibodies.
  • Disease is more prevalent in swampy areas due to insect breeding.
  • Anaemia results from erythrophagocytosis after antibody coating of RBCs.

posts.post_title: Which of the following is the causative agen…
posts.post_content: Which of the following is the causative agent of Equine Influenza?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Type A influenza virus

Equine Influenza is caused by the Type A influenza virus.

Correct Option Explanation

Two serotypes exist based on haemagglutination antigenicity: A/Equi 1 (1956, Czechoslovakia) and A/Equi 2 (1963, Miami, USA).

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Type B influenza is wrong — equine influenza is caused by Type A, not Type B.
  • Herpes virus equi type 4 is wrong — this causes Equine Viral Pneumonitis, not influenza.
  • Arbovirus is wrong — this causes Equine Encephalomyelitis, a different equine disease.
Know More
  • Equine influenza was first recorded in India in 1987.
  • Morbidity can reach 80–100% while mortality is about 0.1%.
  • Equine viral arteritis is differentiated by producing oedema of limbs.
  • Equine rhinopneumonitis mainly affects young horses.

posts.post_title: Caprine Arthritis-Encephalitis (CAE) is caus…
posts.post_content: Caprine Arthritis-Encephalitis (CAE) is caused by which virus?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Lentivirus

CAE is caused by a Lentivirus related to the Maedi-Visna virus.

Correct Option Explanation

It infects cells of the monocyte-macrophage lineage, producing lymphoproliferative lesions in joints or the CNS.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Morbillivirus is wrong — CAE is a lentiviral disease, unlike Rinderpest or PPR.
  • Parvovirus is wrong — parvoviruses cause diseases like Feline Panleucopenia, not CAE.
  • Coronavirus is wrong — coronaviruses cause diseases such as TGE and FIP, not CAE.
Know More
  • CAE was first reported in the United States in 1974.
  • Encephalitic form affects goats aged 1–4 months.
  • Arthritic form is chronic with proliferative synovitis.
  • Diagnosis uses AGID and dot ELISA.

posts.post_title: African Horse Sickness is transmitted by whi…
posts.post_content: African Horse Sickness is transmitted by which vector?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Culicoides mosquitoes

African Horse Sickness (AHS) is transmitted by Culicoides midges.

Correct Option Explanation

AHS is caused by a double-stranded RNA Orbivirus and shows pulmonary (Dunkop) and cardiac (Dikkop) forms.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Aedes mosquitoes is wrong — these transmit the Eastern strain of Equine Encephalomyelitis, not AHS.
  • Ticks is wrong — ticks are not the vector implicated in AHS transmission.
  • Tsetse flies is wrong — these transmit trypanosomiasis, e.g. Nagana, not AHS.
Know More
  • India experienced its worst AHS outbreak in 1960.
  • Cardiac form is called the 'Dikkop' form, meaning thick head.
  • Pulmonary form is called the 'Dunkop' form, meaning thin head.
  • Diagnosis uses intracerebral mouse inoculation and neutralization test.

posts.post_title: Swine Fever produces which characteristic gr…
posts.post_content: Swine Fever produces which characteristic gross lesion in the intestine?

_aimcq_options.text: 'Button ulcers' in the caecum and colon

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 'Button ulcers' in the caecum and colon

Swine Fever produces spherical 'button ulcers' on the mucosa of the caecum and colon.

Correct Option Explanation

These ulcers develop due to infarction following occlusion of small arterioles caused by endothelial swelling and hydropic change.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 'Zebra stripes' is wrong — this pathognomonic lesion is described in Rinderpest and PPR, not Swine Fever.
  • Diphtheritic plaques is wrong — these are found in PPR of small ruminants.
  • Rugae/corrugation is wrong — this is the classic ileal lesion of Johne's disease.
Know More
  • Swine Fever is caused by a Pestivirus of family Togaviridae.
  • Kidney shows a 'Turkey egg' appearance from subcapsular petechiae.
  • The pig is the only domestic animal naturally infected by this virus.
  • First recognised in 1885 in the United States.

posts.post_title: Equine Viral Arteritis is caused by which vi…
posts.post_content: Equine Viral Arteritis is caused by which virus, related to which family?

_aimcq_options.text: Toga virus, related to corona virus

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Toga virus, related to corona virus

Equine Viral Arteritis (EVA) is caused by a Toga virus, now considered related to corona virus.

Correct Option Explanation

Viraemia damages small arteries of the intestine, lymph nodes and adrenals, causing haemorrhagic enteritis and abortion.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Herpes virus is wrong — this causes Equine Viral Pneumonitis, not EVA.
  • Orbivirus is wrong — this causes African Horse Sickness and Bluetongue.
  • Arenavirus is wrong — this is unrelated to EVA and is cited only as a persistent-infection example.
Know More
  • EVA was first reported in the USA in 1957.
  • Carrier stallions can shed virus in semen for up to 2 years.
  • Arterial media is replaced by homogeneous eosinophilic material.
  • Diagnosis uses complement fixation and serum neutralization tests.

posts.post_title: Aujeszky's disease is also known by which sy…
posts.post_content: Aujeszky's disease is also known by which synonym?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Pseudorabies

Aujeszky's disease is also called Pseudorabies or mad itch.

Correct Option Explanation

It is caused by a pantropic herpes virus affecting pigs, cattle, dogs, cats and rodents, first described by Aujeszky in Hungary in 1902.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Swamp fever is wrong — this is a synonym for Equine Infectious Anaemia.
  • Farcy is wrong — this is a synonym for Glanders.
  • Hog cholera is wrong — this is a synonym for Swine Fever.
Know More
  • Pigs and rodents are the natural hosts of the virus.
  • Pruritus (itching) is characteristic in cattle but not seen in pigs.
  • Rabbits show pruritus within 48 hours of experimental inoculation.
  • Intranuclear inclusion bodies occur in degenerated cerebral neurons.

posts.post_title: Swine Influenza virus acts in combination wi…
posts.post_content: Swine Influenza virus acts in combination with which bacterium to produce disease?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Haemophilus influenzae suis

Swine Influenza virus (Type A) acts in combination with the Gram-negative bacterium Haemophilus influenzae suis.

Correct Option Explanation

This virus arose by adaptation of the 1918 human influenza pandemic virus to pigs, and the H1N1 strain persists in pig tissues.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Pasteurella multocida is wrong — this causes secondary pneumonia in swine influenza but is not the defining co-pathogen.
  • Bordetella bronchiseptica is wrong — this is the classic secondary invader in Canine Distemper pneumonia.
  • Actinobacillus lignieresi is wrong — this causes Actinobacillosis (wooden tongue), unrelated to influenza.
Know More
  • Morbidity approaches 100% while mortality is about 1%.
  • Incubation period is 24–48 hours.
  • Lesions show hyaline membrane formation lining alveolar sacs.
  • First appeared in the USA following the 1918 human pandemic.

posts.post_title: Canine Distemper virus belongs to which vira…
posts.post_content: Canine Distemper virus belongs to which viral family?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Paramyxovirus

Canine Distemper is caused by a Paramyxovirus.

Correct Option Explanation

It produces a diphasic fever and, in the CNS, causes demyelinating 'old dog encephalitis' with intracytoplasmic/intranuclear inclusion bodies.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Adenovirus is wrong — this causes Infectious Canine Hepatitis, not distemper.
  • Parvovirus is wrong — this causes Canine Parvoviral Infection, a distinct disease.
  • Rhabdovirus is wrong — this causes Rabies, not distemper.
Know More
  • Distemper is also called Carre's disease or hard pad disease.
  • Hyperkeratosis of digital pads gives the name 'hard pad disease'.
  • Liver shows 'nutmeg' parenchymatous degeneration.
  • Diagnosis uses immunofluorescence on corneal smears.

posts.post_title: In rabies pathogenesis, the virus spreads fr…
posts.post_content: In rabies pathogenesis, the virus spreads from the CNS to the salivary glands mainly via which nerves?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Facial and glossopharyngeal nerves

Rabies virus reaches the salivary glands via the facial (VII) and glossopharyngeal (IX) nerves.

Correct Option Explanation

This affinity allows viral excretion in saliva, enabling transmission through the bite of a rabid animal.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Trigeminal and vagus is wrong — the trigeminal nerve is the route for IBRT spread to the brain, not the rabies salivary route.
  • Optic and olfactory is wrong — these are not the nerves implicated in rabies spread to salivary glands.
  • Sciatic and femoral is wrong — these are peripheral limb nerves, unrelated to salivary gland innervation.
Know More
  • Rabies virus belongs to family Rhabdoviridae.
  • Negri bodies are intracytoplasmic inclusions seen in neurons.
  • Microglial nodules of rabies are called 'Babes nodules'.
  • Cats show only the furious form; rabbits show only the dumb form.

posts.post_title: The 'Fixed virus' of rabies, obtained after…
posts.post_content: The 'Fixed virus' of rabies, obtained after rabbit passage, differs from 'Street virus' in that it is characterized by:

_aimcq_options.text: Short, fixed incubation period and absence of Negri bodies
Long variable incubation period and presence of Negri bodies

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Short, fixed incubation period and absence of Negri bodies

Fixed virus has a short, fixed incubation period and, unlike street virus, lacks Negri bodies.

Correct Option Explanation

Fixed virus kills rabbits by intracerebral inoculation in 7 days and does not affect the salivary glands.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Long variable incubation and Negri bodies present is wrong — these are features of street virus, not fixed virus.
  • Affinity for salivary glands is wrong — this is a street-virus feature; fixed virus does not affect salivary glands.
  • Death in 14–20 days is wrong — this incubation applies to street virus; fixed virus kills in 7 days.
Know More
  • Fixed virus is produced by serial rabbit passage, increasing virulence.
  • Street virus is the form found in natural cases.
  • Habel's mouse inoculation test examines brains on days 5, 6 and 7.
  • Negri bodies are round, acidophilic with basophilic granules.

posts.post_title: Infectious Canine Hepatitis is caused by whi…
posts.post_content: Infectious Canine Hepatitis is caused by which virus?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Canine Adenovirus I

Infectious Canine Hepatitis (Rubarth's disease) is caused by Canine Adenovirus I, a DNA virus.

Correct Option Explanation

Immune complexes formed during infection cause corneal opacity, known as 'Blue eye syndrome'.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Canine Parvovirus is wrong — this causes Canine Parvoviral Infection, a different disease of dogs.
  • Canine Coronavirus is wrong — this causes diarrhoea in young dogs, first reported in 1971.
  • Canine Herpesvirus is not the agent of Rubarth's disease; ICH is caused by an adenovirus.
Know More
  • The disease was fully described by Rubarth in 1947.
  • Thickened, oedematous gall bladder is a pathognomonic gross lesion.
  • Severe hypoglycaemia occurs due to hepatic injury.
  • Large basophilic intranuclear inclusions occur in hepatocytes and endothelium.

posts.post_title: Canine Parvovirus infection was first report…
posts.post_content: Canine Parvovirus infection was first reported in which year?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 1978

Canine Parvovirus (CPV) infection was first reported in 1978.

Correct Option Explanation

Unlike feline panleucopenia virus, CPV does not replicate in cats, and it targets rapidly dividing cells.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 1946 is wrong — this is the year BVD and Mucosal disease were first reported.
  • 1958 is wrong — this is the year the A/Equi 1 equine influenza serotype was first isolated.
  • 1990 is wrong — this is the year Feline Spongiform Encephalopathy was first reported.
Know More
  • Cardiac form affects puppies aged 2–8 weeks.
  • Intestinal form shows necrotising enteritis with intranuclear inclusions.
  • Porcine parvovirus causes intrauterine fetal death and mummification.
  • Bovine parvovirus causes mucoid to watery diarrhoea in calves.

posts.post_title: Feline Panleucopenia is caused by which viru…
posts.post_content: Feline Panleucopenia is caused by which virus?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Parvovirus

Feline Panleucopenia is caused by a Parvovirus that destroys actively dividing cells.

Correct Option Explanation

In kittens infected perinatally, the virus destroys the germinal epithelium of the cerebellum, causing cerebellar hypoplasia.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Coronavirus is wrong — this causes Feline Infectious Peritonitis, not panleucopenia.
  • Herpesvirus is wrong — herpesviruses are not the cause of feline panleucopenia.
  • Calicivirus is wrong — calicivirus causes Vesicular Exanthema of pigs, an unrelated disease.
Know More
  • The disease shows a characteristic diphasic fever.
  • Inclusion bodies are best seen in tissues fixed with Zenker's or Bouin's fixative.
  • It is also called feline distemper or feline agranulocytosis.
  • Diagnosis uses ELISA and haemagglutination inhibition.

posts.post_title: The 'Maedi' component of Visna-Maedi refers…
posts.post_content: The 'Maedi' component of Visna-Maedi refers to which pathological process?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Slowly progressive interstitial pneumonia

Maedi is the slowly progressive interstitial pneumonia form of the visna-maedi lentiviral infection.

Correct Option Explanation

Affected lungs do not collapse on opening the thorax and show a dense, rubbery, grey consistency, 2–5 times normal size.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Slow demyelination is wrong — this describes the 'visna' component, not maedi.
  • Neoplastic transformation is wrong — this describes Jaagsiekte, a distinct retroviral tumour disease of sheep.
  • Non-inflammatory spongiform change is wrong — this describes prion diseases like Scrapie.
Know More
  • Visna and Maedi were both first reported in Iceland (1935 and 1939).
  • Only adult sheep are affected, with a 2–3 year incubation.
  • Intracytoplasmic inclusions appear blue with Giemsa stain in macrophages.
  • Maedi is differentiated from Jaagsiekte on diagnosis.

posts.post_title: Jaagsiekte is caused by which type of virus?
posts.post_content: Jaagsiekte is caused by which type of virus?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Type D oncovirus (retrovirus)

Jaagsiekte, or ovine pulmonary adenomatosis, is caused by a Type D oncovirus, a retrovirus.

Correct Option Explanation

The virus transforms Type II pneumocytes and Clara cells into neoplastic adenomatous growths in the alveoli and bronchioles.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Lentivirus is wrong — lentivirus causes Visna-Maedi, a different chronic sheep lung disease.
  • Prion is wrong — prions cause Scrapie, a spongiform encephalopathy, not a lung tumour.
  • Herpesvirus is wrong — herpesviruses are not implicated in Jaagsiekte.
Know More
  • The 'Wheel barrow test' demonstrates watery nasal discharge on lifting the hind legs.
  • Disease affects sheep aged 3–4 years, with death in 6 weeks to 4 months.
  • Pasteurellosis is a common secondary complication.
  • First reported in South Africa.

posts.post_title: Scrapie is caused by which type of infectiou…
posts.post_content: Scrapie is caused by which type of infectious agent?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Prion (proteinaceous infectious particle)

Scrapie is caused by a prion, a proteinaceous infectious particle lacking DNA or RNA.

Correct Option Explanation

The normal cellular prion protein (PrPc) undergoes a conformational change from an alpha-helix to a beta-pleated sheet (PrPsc).

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Retrovirus is wrong — retroviruses cause diseases like Jaagsiekte, not scrapie.
  • Herpesvirus is wrong — herpesviruses are not implicated in the transmissible spongiform encephalopathies.
  • Pestivirus is wrong — pestiviruses cause diseases like Swine Fever and BVD.
Know More
  • Prions produce no inflammation or immune reaction in the host.
  • Scrapie was first recorded in Britain in 1732.
  • Lesions show spongiosis and astrocyte hyperplasia in grey matter.
  • An eyelid test was developed in the US for live-animal diagnosis.

posts.post_title: Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE) was f…
posts.post_content: Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE) was first reported in which year and country?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 1986, Britain

BSE ('Mad Cow Disease') was first reported in 1986 in a British dairy herd.

Correct Option Explanation

It is caused by an abnormal prion protein and has an unusually long incubation period of about 4–5 years.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 1990, England is wrong — this is the year Feline Spongiform Encephalopathy was first reported.
  • 1946, Canada is wrong — this is the year Mucosal disease was first reported.
  • 1902, South Africa is wrong — this is the year Blue Tongue was first recognised.
Know More
  • Transmission occurs via feeding of meat and bone meal to cattle.
  • Mostly female cattle are affected.
  • Microscopic lesions show ballooned neurons and gliosis.
  • Clinical signs last 2 weeks to 6 months before death.

posts.post_title: Feline Spongiform Encephalopathy is transmit…
posts.post_content: Feline Spongiform Encephalopathy is transmitted mainly by which route?

_aimcq_options.text: Consumption of bovine offal from BSE-affected cattle

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Consumption of bovine offal from BSE-affected cattle

Feline Spongiform Encephalopathy is transmitted by consumption of bovine offal from cattle affected with BSE.

Correct Option Explanation

It was first reported in England in 1990 and mainly affects older cats, with cytoplasmic vacuolation of neurons.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Bite of an infected cat is wrong — the disease is dietary in origin, not spread by biting.
  • Placental transmission is wrong — this route is not described for Feline Spongiform Encephalopathy.
  • Insect vector is wrong — no insect vector is implicated in this prion disease.
Know More
  • Clinical signs include tremors, ataxia and behavioural change.
  • Fibrils and modified prion proteins are found in affected brains.
  • Scrapie is the prototype prion disease of sheep and goats.
  • BSE and Scrapie share prion-based pathogenesis.

posts.post_title: Vesicular Exanthema of swine is caused by wh…
posts.post_content: Vesicular Exanthema of swine is caused by which type of virus?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Calicivirus

Vesicular Exanthema of swine is caused by a Calicivirus.

Correct Option Explanation

It was first reported in 1935 in California, USA, and produces vesicles on the snout, tongue and coronary band, similar to FMD.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Picorna virus is wrong — this causes FMD, a differential diagnosis, not Vesicular Exanthema.
  • Rhabdovirus is wrong — this causes Vesicular Stomatitis.
  • Poxvirus is wrong — poxviruses cause diseases such as Swine pox, not Vesicular Exanthema.
Know More
  • Viraemia lasts 72–84 hours before localizing in buccal mucosa and skin.
  • Guinea pigs are not naturally infected (per the vesicular disease susceptibility table).
  • Diagnosis uses complement fixation and virus neutralization tests.
  • Abortion may occur in lactating sows.

posts.post_title: Which laboratory finding differentiates Vesi…
posts.post_content: Which laboratory finding differentiates Vesicular Stomatitis from FMD?

_aimcq_options.text: Vesicular stomatitis can only be produced in cattle by lingual, not intramuscular, inoculation
Vesicular stomatitis produces myocardial 'Tigroid heart' lesions
Vesicular stomatitis has high mortality in cattle
Vesicular stomatitis is caused by a Picorna virus

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Vesicular stomatitis can only be produced in cattle by lingual, not intramuscular, inoculation

Vesicular Stomatitis can be reproduced in cattle only by the lingual route, unlike FMD which is producible by intramuscular inoculation.

Correct Option Explanation

Vesicular stomatitis is caused by a Rhabdovirus and shows no myocardial lesions and very low mortality.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 'Tigroid heart' is wrong — this myocardial lesion is characteristic of FMD, not vesicular stomatitis.
  • High mortality in cattle is wrong — vesicular stomatitis causes very low or no mortality in cattle.
  • Picorna virus is wrong — vesicular stomatitis is caused by a Rhabdovirus, not a Picorna virus.
Know More
  • Three antigenic strains exist: New Jersey, Indiana and Trinidad.
  • Vector transmission involves mosquitoes, black flies, gnats and midges.
  • Goats and sheep are relatively resistant to the disease.
  • Healing of lesions usually occurs in 7–10 days.

posts.post_title: Lumpy Skin Disease of cattle is caused by a…
posts.post_content: Lumpy Skin Disease of cattle is caused by a virus related to which viral group?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Sheep and goat pox viruses

Lumpy Skin Disease is caused by a Capripox virus, related to sheep and goat pox viruses.

Correct Option Explanation

It was first reported in Zambia in 1929 and spreads mainly by insect vectors such as flies.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Vaccinia virus is wrong — vaccinia is the virus used for human smallpox immunisation, unrelated to LSD.
  • Bovine papular stomatitis virus is wrong — this is a parapoxvirus, a different genus from Capripox.
  • Bluetongue virus is wrong — Bluetongue is an orbivirus, unrelated to Lumpy Skin Disease.
Know More
  • Mortality rate is around 10%.
  • Eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusion bodies occur in keratinocytes and fibroblasts.
  • Nodules also occur on oral, nasal and genital mucous membranes.
  • Diagnosis uses electron microscopy and serum neutralization test.

posts.post_title: Cowpox virus is most closely related to whic…
posts.post_content: Cowpox virus is most closely related to which other viruses?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Variola and vaccinia viruses

Cowpox virus is closely related to, but distinct from, the variola and vaccinia viruses.

Correct Option Explanation

The disease is mild and self-limiting, with lesions mainly confined to the teats and udder.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Capripox viruses is wrong — these cause sheep, goat and lumpy skin disease, a different pox genus.
  • Parapoxviruses is wrong — these cause Orf and Bovine Papular Stomatitis, unrelated to Cowpox.
  • Suipox virus is wrong — this causes Swine pox, a genetically distinct virus.
Know More
  • Cowpox has an unusually wide host range.
  • Buffalo pox has been reported in India, Indonesia, Pakistan, Egypt, Italy and Russia.
  • Camel pox is generalized and often fatal in young camels.
  • Monkey pox was first identified in Denmark in 1958.

posts.post_title: Contagious Pustular Dermatitis (Orf) of shee…
posts.post_content: Contagious Pustular Dermatitis (Orf) of sheep and goats is caused by which virus?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Parapox virus

Orf is caused by a Parapox virus, immunologically related to bovine papular stomatitis virus.

Correct Option Explanation

Lesions begin at the oral commissures and spread to the muzzle, with eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions in keratinocytes.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Capripox virus is wrong — this causes sheep pox and goat pox, distinct systemic pox diseases.
  • Suipox virus is wrong — this causes Swine pox, a disease of pigs.
  • Herpesvirus is wrong — herpesviruses are unrelated to Orf's parapoxvirus aetiology.
Know More
  • Outbreaks are more common in spring and summer.
  • Scabs remain infective for long periods in the environment.
  • The disease is more severe in lambs and kids.
  • Diagnosis uses agar gel immunodiffusion and electron microscopy.

posts.post_title: In Sheep Pox, the distinctive cells found in…
posts.post_content: In Sheep Pox, the distinctive cells found in the oedematous dermis around blood vessels are called:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 'Sheep pox cells' (cellules claveleuses of Borrel)

Sheep pox produces distinctive 'sheep pox cells', also called cellules claveleuses of Borrel, around vessels in the dermis.

Correct Option Explanation

These cells contain intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies and are also found in pneumonic alveolar septal cells, the key visceral lesion.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Negri bodies is wrong — these are intracytoplasmic inclusions found in rabies-infected neurons.
  • Langhans giant cells is wrong — these are found in tuberculosis granulomas.
  • Sulphur granules is wrong — these are colonies of organisms seen in Actinomycosis/Actinobacillosis.
Know More
  • Sheep pox is caused by a Capripox virus.
  • Mortality is 50% in adults and 100% in lambs.
  • Goat pox has a longer incubation period and is milder than sheep pox.
  • Diagnosis uses fluorescent antibody test and immunodiffusion.

posts.post_title: Swine pox is transmitted mainly by which vec…
posts.post_content: Swine pox is transmitted mainly by which vector?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Swine louse (Haematopinus suis)

Swine pox is transmitted mainly by the swine louse, Haematopinus suis.

Correct Option Explanation

It is caused by a Suipox virus and produces a benign disease with typical pox lesions on the ventral abdomen.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Culicoides midges is wrong — these transmit Bluetongue and African Horse Sickness, not swine pox.
  • Aedes mosquitoes is wrong — these transmit the eastern strain of Equine Encephalomyelitis.
  • Ixodes ticks is wrong — Ixodes ricinus is linked to tick pyaemia in lambs, not swine pox.
Know More
  • Incubation period of swine pox is 5–7 days.
  • Solid immunity develops after natural infection.
  • Eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusion bodies occur in epithelial cells.
  • Lesions favour the underside of the body and inner limbs.

posts.post_title: Bovine Papular Stomatitis of young cattle is…
posts.post_content: Bovine Papular Stomatitis of young cattle is caused by which virus?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Parapox virus

Bovine Papular Stomatitis is a mild disease of young calves caused by a Parapox virus.

Correct Option Explanation

Lesions begin as foci of hyperaemia at the nostril margins or lips and develop into whitish papules within a day.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Capripox virus is wrong — this causes systemic pox diseases like Lumpy Skin Disease, not this mild stomatitis.
  • Adenovirus is wrong — adenoviruses cause diseases like Infectious Canine Hepatitis, unrelated to this condition.
  • Coronavirus is wrong — coronaviruses cause enteric diseases such as TGE, not this stomatitis.
Know More
  • Lesions also occur in the oesophagus, rumen, reticulum and omasum.
  • Microscopic change includes hydropic degeneration with eosinophilic inclusions.
  • The disease is also called infectious ulcerative stomatitis and oesophagitis.
  • Susceptible animals are mainly young calves.

posts.post_title: In Equine Encephalomyelitis, the Eastern str…
posts.post_content: In Equine Encephalomyelitis, the Eastern strain is transmitted to horses mainly by which vector?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Aedes mosquitoes

The Eastern strain of equine encephalomyelitis virus infects birds and is transmitted to horses via Aedes mosquitoes.

Correct Option Explanation

This arbovirus causes non-suppurative encephalitis and profound behavioural changes such as blindness and circling.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Culex mosquitoes is wrong — these transmit the Western strain, not the Eastern strain.
  • Culicoides midges is wrong — these transmit Bluetongue and AHS, not equine encephalomyelitis.
  • Ixodes ticks is wrong — ticks are not the vector for equine encephalomyelitis.
Know More
  • Three strains exist: Eastern, Western and Venezuelan.
  • Viraemia is transient in Eastern/Western strains but persistent in Venezuelan strain.
  • Chick embryo inoculation causes death within 18–24 hours.
  • The synonym for this disease is 'blind staggers'.

posts.post_title: Neonatal Calf Diarrhoea caused by Group A ro…
posts.post_content: Neonatal Calf Diarrhoea caused by Group A rotavirus mainly affects which intestinal cells?

_aimcq_options.text: Mature, differentiated columnar epithelial cells of villi

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Mature, differentiated columnar epithelial cells of villi

Group A rotavirus infects only the mature, differentiated columnar epithelial cells lining the apical halves of intestinal villi.

Correct Option Explanation

This causes necrosis, sloughing, villous stunting and compensatory hypertrophy of enterocytes in the crypts.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Undifferentiated crypt cells is wrong — these are spared by Group A rotavirus and instead proliferate to replace lost villous cells.
  • Goblet cells of the colon is wrong — rotavirus targets the small intestinal villous epithelium, not colonic goblet cells.
  • Paneth cells is wrong — these are not the target cell population described for rotaviral enteritis.
Know More
  • Group B rotavirus causes syncytia on the villous surface instead.
  • Susceptible calves are typically around 2 weeks old.
  • Immunofluorescent staining of faeces works up to 4–6 hours.
  • Electron microscopy detects virus in faeces for 6–10 days.

posts.post_title: Transmissible Gastroenteritis (TGE) of swine…
posts.post_content: Transmissible Gastroenteritis (TGE) of swine is antigenically related to which other viruses?

_aimcq_options.text: Feline infectious peritonitis and canine corona virus

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Feline infectious peritonitis and canine corona virus

TGE virus, a corona virus, is antigenically related to feline infectious peritonitis and canine corona virus.

Correct Option Explanation

It infects mature columnar villous epithelial cells (sparing crypt cells), causing marked villous atrophy mainly in the jejunum.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Rotavirus and reovirus is wrong — TGE virus is a coronavirus, antigenically distinct from these.
  • Parvovirus and adenovirus is wrong — these are unrelated DNA virus families, not linked to TGE.
  • Pestivirus and lentivirus is wrong — TGE virus is a coronavirus, not related to these genera.
Know More
  • Mortality can reach 100% in piglets under 10 days of age.
  • TGE was first described in 1946.
  • Replication in villous cells occurs within 4–5 hours.
  • Diagnosis uses ELISA, IFT, IPT and neutralization test.

posts.post_title: Feline Infectious Peritonitis (FIP) is cause…
posts.post_content: Feline Infectious Peritonitis (FIP) is caused by which virus and shows which two clinical forms?

_aimcq_options.text: Corona virus; wet and dry forms

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Corona virus; wet and dry forms

FIP is caused by a Corona virus and presents as either a 'wet' (effusive) or 'dry' (non-effusive) form.

Correct Option Explanation

The wet form causes excessive fibrinous fluid accumulation of up to 1 litre in the abdominal cavity, with granulomatous vasculitis.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Parvovirus; acute/chronic is wrong — FIP is caused by a coronavirus, and its forms are described as wet/dry, not acute/chronic.
  • Herpesvirus is wrong — herpesviruses do not cause FIP.
  • Calicivirus is wrong — calicivirus is unrelated to feline peritoneal effusion disease.
Know More
  • Disease has a slowly progressive course of one to several months.
  • Vasculitis is immune-mediated in pathogenesis.
  • Multiple necrotic foci occur in liver, spleen and kidney.
  • Cats of all ages are susceptible worldwide.

posts.post_title: General pathology of bacterial infection: li…
posts.post_content: General pathology of bacterial infection: lipopolysaccharide (LPS) endotoxin is a structural component of which part of the bacterial cell?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Cell wall of Gram-negative bacteria

LPS (endotoxin) is a complex component of the cell wall of Gram-negative bacteria.

Correct Option Explanation

LPS consists of toxic lipid A joined to a core sugar chain and an O antigen carbohydrate chain used for serotyping.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Gram-positive cell wall is wrong — LPS is specifically a Gram-negative cell wall component, absent in Gram-positive organisms.
  • Flagella is wrong — flagella are motility organelles, not the source of endotoxin.
  • Capsule only is wrong — the capsule is a distinct virulence structure and not synonymous with LPS.
Know More
  • LPS activates macrophages to release IL-1 and TNF.
  • High LPS levels can cause septic/endotoxic shock and DIC.
  • LPS-protein complexes bind CD14 on leukocytes.
  • Exotoxins, by contrast, are secreted, heat-labile bacterial proteins.

posts.post_title: Which neurotoxin is produced by Clostridium…
posts.post_content: Which neurotoxin is produced by Clostridium tetani and blocks inhibitory neurotransmitters?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Tetanospasmin

Tetanospasmin, the neurotoxin of Clostridium tetani, blocks inhibitory transmitter substances, causing spastic paralysis.

Correct Option Explanation

The toxin binds to a substance called 'protagon' at inhibitory synapses, producing hyperirritability and tetanic spasms.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Tetanolysin is wrong — this is a haemolysin produced by Cl. tetani but is not the neurotoxin responsible for spasms.
  • Botulinum toxin is wrong — this is produced by Cl. botulinum and blocks cholinergic transmission, causing flaccid paralysis.
  • Alpha toxin is wrong — this is produced by Cl. perfringens and causes haemolysis and cell membrane damage.
Know More
  • Tetanus spores have a characteristic 'drum stick' shape.
  • Horses and mules are highly susceptible to tetanus.
  • Clinical sign in horses is stiffness, described as 'wooden horse' gait.
  • No characteristic gross lesion is seen; death is due to toxaemia.

posts.post_title: Which mycobacterial species causes Johne's d…
posts.post_content: Which mycobacterial species causes Johne's disease in cattle and sheep?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Mycobacterium paratuberculosis

Johne's disease (paratuberculosis) is caused by Mycobacterium paratuberculosis.

Correct Option Explanation

Three strains exist — bovine, ovine and Scottish — producing chronic granulomatous enteritis after ingestion.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • M. bovis is wrong — this causes bovine tuberculosis, a distinct mycobacterial disease.
  • M. avium is wrong — this causes tuberculosis in domestic and wild fowl, pigs and monkeys.
  • M. leprae is wrong — this causes human leprosy, unrelated to Johne's disease.
Know More
  • Incubation period can be as long as 2 years.
  • Ileal mucosa shows transverse corrugation, resembling cerebral convolutions.
  • Diagnosis includes the Johnin test, CFT, AGID and ELISA.
  • Corrugation is less marked in sheep and goats than cattle.

posts.post_title: In tuberculosis, the characteristic giant ce…
posts.post_content: In tuberculosis, the characteristic giant cells formed by fusion of macrophages, with nuclei arranged in a horseshoe pattern, are called:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Langhans' giant cells

Fusion of epithelioid macrophages in tuberculosis forms Langhans' giant cells, with peripheral horseshoe-arranged nuclei.

Correct Option Explanation

These, with a zone of lymphocytes and fibroblasts, constitute the classic tubercle granuloma caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Sheep pox cells is wrong — these (cellules claveleuses) are seen in Sheep pox, unrelated to TB.
  • Negri bodies is wrong — these are viral inclusions of rabies, not TB granulomas.
  • Reticulo-endothelial nodules is wrong — this generic term does not describe the specific TB giant cell.
Know More
  • The cord factor of M. tuberculosis promotes granuloma formation.
  • Acid-fastness is due to the mycolic acid fraction.
  • Ziehl-Neelsen's stain demonstrates acid-fast rods.
  • Pigs show TB confined mainly to cervical lymph nodes of the head.

posts.post_title: Which pathogenesis-defining lesion of Actino…
posts.post_content: Which pathogenesis-defining lesion of Actinomycosis (lumpy jaw) forms centrally within the granuloma?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 'Sulphur granules' (colonies of organisms)

Actinomycosis produces yellowish pus containing 'sulphur granules', which are colonies of the causative organism.

Correct Option Explanation

Actinomyces bovis, a Gram-positive branching anaerobe, produces rarefying osteomyelitis, classically of the mandible ('lumpy jaw').

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Negri bodies is wrong — these are rabies viral inclusions, unrelated to bacterial granulomas.
  • Zebra stripes is wrong — this describes haemorrhagic mucosal streaking in Rinderpest/PPR.
  • Button ulcers is wrong — this describes intestinal lesions of Swine Fever.
Know More
  • Horses show poll evil and fistulous withers from actinomycosis-like infection.
  • Involucrum forms as new subperiosteal bone around the lesion.
  • Actinobacillosis, by contrast, mainly affects the tongue ('wooden tongue').
  • Actinobacillus lignieresi is the agent of wooden tongue disease.

posts.post_title: Actinobacillosis (Wooden Tongue) of cattle i…
posts.post_content: Actinobacillosis (Wooden Tongue) of cattle is caused by which organism?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Actinobacillus lignieresi

Actinobacillosis, or 'wooden tongue', is caused by Actinobacillus lignieresi, a Gram-negative aerobe.

Correct Option Explanation

Infection produces chronic suppurative granulomatous inflammation, mainly of the tongue, causing it to become hard and immobile.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Actinomyces bovis is wrong — this Gram-positive organism causes Actinomycosis (lumpy jaw), mainly of bone.
  • Mycobacterium bovis is wrong — this causes bovine tuberculosis, unrelated to wooden tongue.
  • Fusobacterium necrophorum is not the agent described for wooden tongue in this text.
Know More
  • Organisms are normal inhabitants of the upper respiratory and alimentary tract.
  • Sheep show subcutaneous granulomas of the head rather than lingual lesions.
  • Diffuse sclerosing actinobacillosis affects the tongue specifically.
  • Diagnosis uses pus smear examination and agglutination test.

posts.post_title: Anthrax is caused by which organism?
posts.post_content: Anthrax is caused by which organism?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Bacillus anthracis

Anthrax is caused by Bacillus anthracis, a Gram-positive, capsulated, spore-forming rod.

Correct Option Explanation

Toxin factors include oedema factor, protective antigen and lethal factor, producing haemorrhage and rapid death.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Clostridium chauvoei is wrong — this causes Black Quarter, a different acute clostridial disease.
  • Clostridium septicum is wrong — this causes Braxy and gas gangrene, not anthrax.
  • Bacillus cereus is wrong — this is not identified as the anthrax agent in veterinary pathology.
Know More
  • Postmortem examination of anthrax carcasses should be avoided to prevent sporulation.
  • The capsule is demonstrated by McFadyen's reaction.
  • Human cutaneous anthrax is called 'Malignant Carbuncle'.
  • Ascoli precipitation test gives a white precipitate for confirmation.

posts.post_title: In anthrax, spores are said to form only aft…
posts.post_content: In anthrax, spores are said to form only after the carcass is opened because:

_aimcq_options.text: Spores do not form inside living tissue but form on contact with atmospheric oxygen
Anthrax bacilli are naturally aspore genic
Spore formation requires host antibody stimulation

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Spores do not form inside living tissue but form on contact with atmospheric oxygen

Anthrax spores do not form inside a living or unopened animal but form once the carcass is opened and organisms contact atmospheric oxygen.

Correct Option Explanation

This is why postmortem examination of suspected anthrax carcasses is avoided — opening spreads sporulating, environmentally resistant organisms.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Requires refrigeration is wrong — sporulation is triggered by exposure to air/oxygen, not temperature.
  • Naturally aspore genic is wrong — B. anthracis is a spore-forming organism; it simply does not sporulate in vivo.
  • Requires host antibody is wrong — sporulation is an environmental response, unrelated to host immunity.
Know More
  • Sheep and cattle are the most susceptible species.
  • Death may occur within 12–36 hours in the peracute form.
  • Man may develop 'Wool sorters' disease' from contact with hides.
  • Fluorescent antibody technique aids confirmatory diagnosis.

posts.post_title: Exudative Epidermitis of swine (Greasy Pig D…
posts.post_content: Exudative Epidermitis of swine (Greasy Pig Disease) is caused by which organism?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Staphylococcus aureus

Exudative Epidermitis (Greasy Pig Disease) is an acute generalized seborrhoeic dermatitis caused by Staphylococcus aureus.

Correct Option Explanation

Suckling piglets are affected, with sudden cutaneous erythema and death within 24–48 hours in the peracute form.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Streptococcus suis is wrong — this causes streptococcal meningitis and arthritis in young pigs, not greasy pig disease.
  • Actinobacillus lignieresi is wrong — this causes wooden tongue, unrelated to skin disease.
  • Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae is not identified in this text as the cause of exudative epidermitis.
Know More
  • Gilts and sows act as carriers of the organism.
  • Chronic form shows thickened skin with thick scabs.
  • Botryomycosis is another S. aureus-associated pyogranulomatous disease.
  • Diagnosis relies on isolation and identification of S. aureus.

posts.post_title: In Botryomycosis, the eosinophilic 'rosettes…
posts.post_content: In Botryomycosis, the eosinophilic 'rosettes' seen in tissue sections are also known as:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Splendore-Hoeppli material

The eosinophilic rosettes surrounding bacterial colonies in Botryomycosis are called Splendore-Hoeppli material.

Correct Option Explanation

This chronic pyogranulomatous disease is caused by Staphylococcus aureus and grossly seen as firm nodules with 'grains'.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Negri bodies is wrong — these are rabies viral inclusions in neurons, unrelated to botryomycosis.
  • Sulphur granules is wrong — while grossly similar in appearance, this specific term is used for Actinomycosis/Actinobacillosis colonies.
  • Cellules claveleuses is wrong — this term describes sheep pox cells, an unrelated viral lesion.
Know More
  • Cattle mammary glands and horse castration wounds are common sites.
  • Gram's stain reveals colonies of cocci surrounded by rosettes.
  • The lesion is a chronic pyogranulomatous inflammation.
  • It is caused by the same organism as exudative epidermitis of swine.

posts.post_title: Strangles in horses is caused by which organ…
posts.post_content: Strangles in horses is caused by which organism?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Streptococcus equi

Strangles is caused by Streptococcus equi, producing mucopurulent respiratory infection and lymph node abscessation.

Correct Option Explanation

Abscesses in retropharyngeal lymph nodes can drain into the guttural pouches, causing empyema.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Streptococcus suis is wrong — this causes streptococcal meningitis and arthritis in pigs, not strangles in horses.
  • Staphylococcus aureus is wrong — this causes conditions like botryomycosis and greasy pig disease.
  • Actinobacillus lignieresi is wrong — this causes wooden tongue, a granulomatous lingual disease.
Know More
  • Incubation period is 4–8 days.
  • 'Purpura haemorrhagica' can follow strangles due to hypersensitivity.
  • Unilateral nasal discharge suggests glanders, not strangles.
  • Death may result from septicaemia and pyaemia.

posts.post_title: Black Quarter (Black Leg) of cattle is cause…
posts.post_content: Black Quarter (Black Leg) of cattle is caused by which organism?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Clostridium chauvoei

Black Quarter is caused by Clostridium chauvoei, a Gram-positive, spore-forming rod.

Correct Option Explanation

Ingested spores reach the muscle via blood, producing necrotising myositis with gas and a rancid butter odour.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Clostridium septicum is wrong — this causes Braxy and gas gangrene, distinct from Black Quarter.
  • Cl. novyi type B is wrong — this causes Black Disease (infectious necrotic hepatitis).
  • Cl. haemolyticum is wrong — this causes Bacillary Haemoglobinuria (Red Water Disease).
Know More
  • Affected muscle turns black from iron sulphide formation.
  • Disease mainly affects cattle aged 6 months to 2 years.
  • Sheep may acquire it through wound infection.
  • Mortality in enzootic areas may approach 100%.

posts.post_title: Bovine Bacillary Haemoglobinuria (Red Water…
posts.post_content: Bovine Bacillary Haemoglobinuria (Red Water Disease) is caused by which organism, activated by which predisposing condition?

_aimcq_options.text: Clostridium haemolyticum; liver fluke migration damage
Clostridium novyi type B; anaerobic wound

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Clostridium haemolyticum; liver fluke migration damage

Bacillary Haemoglobinuria is caused by Clostridium haemolyticum, activated by hepatic damage such as liver fluke migration.

Correct Option Explanation

The organism's beta toxin causes further necrotic hepatic infarcts and severe intravascular haemolysis.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Cl. chauvoei; muscle injury is wrong — this describes Black Quarter, a myonecrotic disease, not haemoglobinuria.
  • Cl. septicum; frozen grass is wrong — this describes Braxy, an abomasal disease of sheep.
  • Cl. novyi type B; anaerobic wound is wrong — this organism causes Black Disease, a hepatic necrosis of sheep.
Know More
  • Haemoglobin can fall as low as 3 g/dL in acute cases.
  • First described in California in 1916.
  • Urine is deep red in colour from haemoglobinuria.
  • Cattle are mostly susceptible; sheep and swine are rarely affected.

posts.post_title: Braxy of sheep is caused by which organism a…
posts.post_content: Braxy of sheep is caused by which organism and affects which organ primarily?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Clostridium septicum; abomasum

Braxy is caused by Clostridium septicum and primarily produces haemorrhagic abomasitis.

Correct Option Explanation

Toxins are liberated after organisms enter through abomasal wounds caused by nematodes or the ingestion of frozen, chilled grass.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Cl. novyi; liver is wrong — this describes Black Disease, a hepatic infection, not abomasal disease.
  • Cl. chauvoei; skeletal muscle is wrong — this describes Black Quarter, a myonecrotic disease.
  • Cl. tetani; nervous system is wrong — this describes Tetanus, a neurotoxic disease.
Know More
  • Braxy is mainly seen in Scotland and Scandinavia.
  • Death occurs within a few hours of colic and abomasal bloat.
  • Also known by the synonym 'Bradsot'.
  • Large bacilli are visible in tissue sections.

posts.post_title: Black Disease (Infectious Necrotic Hepatitis…
posts.post_content: Black Disease (Infectious Necrotic Hepatitis) of sheep is activated by the migration of which parasite?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Liver flukes

Black Disease is caused by Clostridium novyi type B, activated in an anaerobic niche created by migrating liver flukes.

Correct Option Explanation

The released exotoxin causes multiple hepatic necrotic foci, and subcutaneous venous congestion gives the skin its dark, black colour.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Ancylostoma is wrong — this is a hookworm affecting the intestine, not implicated in Black Disease.
  • Moniezia is wrong — this is an intestinal tapeworm, unrelated to hepatic clostridial activation.
  • Trypanosoma is wrong — this is a blood protozoan parasite, unrelated to hepatic fluke damage.
Know More
  • First reported in Australia, later New Zealand and elsewhere.
  • Petechiae occur on the epicardium and endocardium.
  • Hydropericardium is a common associated finding.
  • Faecal contamination by carriers is the main infection source.

posts.post_title: Clostridium perfringens type D causes which…
posts.post_content: Clostridium perfringens type D causes which disease, also known as 'Overeating Disease'?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Pulpy Kidney Disease

Clostridium perfringens type D causes Pulpy Kidney Disease, also called 'overeating disease' of fattening lambs.

Correct Option Explanation

Excessive starch feeding allows organism proliferation; the absorbed epsilon toxin produces toxaemia, convulsions and coma.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Lamb dysentery is wrong — this is caused by Cl. perfringens type B, producing haemorrhagic enteritis.
  • Struck is wrong — this is caused by Cl. perfringens type C in adult sheep.
  • Black Disease is wrong — this is caused by Cl. novyi type B, a hepatic disease.
Know More
  • Kidneys become swollen and pulpy, giving the disease its name.
  • Hyperglycaemia and glycosuria are diagnostic supporting signs.
  • A mouse neutralization test confirms the specific toxin type.
  • Enterotoxaemia has also been reported in calves.

posts.post_title: Botulism results from which mechanism of dis…
posts.post_content: Botulism results from which mechanism of disease production?

_aimcq_options.text: Ingestion of preformed exotoxin in food
Direct bacterial invasion of nerve tissue

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Ingestion of preformed exotoxin in food

Botulism results from ingestion of preformed exotoxin produced by Clostridium botulinum in food, not from bacterial invasion.

Correct Option Explanation

The toxin blocks the release of acetylcholine at peripheral nerves, causing flaccid paralysis, but does not enter the CNS.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Direct bacterial invasion is wrong — the organism itself does not need to invade tissue; only preformed toxin is required.
  • Endotoxin release is wrong — botulinum toxin is a classic exotoxin, not an endotoxin.
  • Immune complex deposition is wrong — this mechanism is unrelated to botulism's neuroparalytic toxin action.
Know More
  • Type A causes 'Limber neck' in poultry.
  • Type C causes forage poisoning in horses.
  • Type E is associated with fish and fish products.
  • Swine are relatively resistant since the toxin is poorly absorbed.

posts.post_title: Glanders in horses is caused by which organi…
posts.post_content: Glanders in horses is caused by which organism?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Pseudomonas mallei (Actinobacillus mallei)

Glanders is caused by Pseudomonas mallei, also called Actinobacillus mallei.

Correct Option Explanation

It produces nodules and ulcers of the upper airways, lungs and skin, with thick tortuous lymphatics called 'farcy cords'.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Streptococcus equi is wrong — this causes Strangles, which shows bilateral, not unilateral, nasal discharge.
  • Bacillus anthracis is wrong — this causes Anthrax, a septicaemic disease, not glanders.
  • Clostridium chauvoei is wrong — this causes Black Quarter, a myonecrotic disease, unrelated to glanders.
Know More
  • Unilateral nasal discharge is characteristic of glanders.
  • The synonym for the disease is 'Farcy'.
  • The Straus test uses guinea pig inoculation showing suppurative orchitis.
  • Confirmation uses the intradermal mallein test.

posts.post_title: Haemorrhagic Septicaemia of cattle and buffa…
posts.post_content: Haemorrhagic Septicaemia of cattle and buffalo is caused by which organism?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Pasteurella boviseptica

Haemorrhagic Septicaemia in cattle and buffalo is caused by Pasteurella boviseptica.

Correct Option Explanation

It produces sudden high fever, hot painful throat/brisket swelling and petechial haemorrhages on serous and mucous membranes.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • P. avi septica is wrong — this causes fowl cholera in birds, not cattle haemorrhagic septicaemia.
  • P. sui septica is wrong — this causes swine plague, a related but distinct pasteurellosis.
  • P. pestis is wrong — this causes bubonic plague in man, with rat as natural host.
Know More
  • The bipolar rod appearance is a key microscopic feature.
  • Rabbit inoculation causes death within 24–40 hours with haemorrhagic tracheitis.
  • Also known as 'stockyards disease' or 'barbone'.
  • Fibrinous bronchopneumonia is the predominant lung lesion.

posts.post_title: The characteristic microscopic staining feat…
posts.post_content: The characteristic microscopic staining feature of Pasteurella organisms is called:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Bipolar appearance

Pasteurella organisms show a bipolar appearance, with the ends of the ovoid rods staining more deeply than the centre.

Correct Option Explanation

This is seen classically in Haemorrhagic Septicaemia of cattle and in fowl cholera caused by related Pasteurella species.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Beaded appearance is wrong — this describes leucocyte infiltration patterns seen in Glanders nodules.
  • Rosette formation is wrong — this describes the Splendore-Hoeppli material of Botryomycosis.
  • Club-like structure is wrong — this describes the granuloma reaction in Actinomycosis/Actinobacillosis.
Know More
  • Mannheimia haemolytica causes arthritis in calves and mastitis in ewes/cows.
  • All pasteurella types are grouped under 'Pasteurella multocida'.
  • Fowl cholera causes enlargement of liver and spleen.
  • Shipping fever involves both bacterial and viral stress factors.

posts.post_title: Shipping Fever in transported calves is prec…
posts.post_content: Shipping Fever in transported calves is precipitated by which combination of factors?

_aimcq_options.text: Stress plus viral and bacterial infections

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Stress plus viral and bacterial infections

Shipping Fever is a multifactorial disease precipitated by stress combined with viral and bacterial infections.

Correct Option Explanation

Contributing viruses include Parainfluenza-3 and IBR virus, while Pasteurella multocida and other bacteria cause secondary lesions.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Vitamin A deficiency alone is wrong — nutritional deficiency is not described as the cause of shipping fever.
  • Prion accumulation is wrong — prions cause degenerative CNS disease, unrelated to shipping fever.
  • Fungal toxin ingestion is wrong — mycotoxins are a separate category of disease, not implicated here.
Know More
  • Stress factors include heat, cold, fatigue and insufficient feed/water.
  • Oedema and haemorrhage occur in the upper nasal passage and larynx.
  • Bovine adenovirus is also cited as a contributing viral agent.
  • Regional lymph nodes are typically affected.

posts.post_title: Leptospirosis in dogs is most commonly cause…
posts.post_content: Leptospirosis in dogs is most commonly caused by which two Leptospira serovars?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: L. canicola and L. icterohaemorrhagiae

Canine leptospirosis is most commonly caused by L. canicola and L. icterohaemorrhagiae.

Correct Option Explanation

Rats act as reservoirs transmitting infection to dogs, producing nephritis (canicola) and jaundice (icterohaemorrhagiae).

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • L. pomona and L. grippotyphosa is wrong — these serovars are associated with swine/cattle and goats, respectively.
  • L. hardjo and L. bratislava is wrong — these serovars are not the ones named in this text for dogs.
  • L. australis and L. javanica is wrong — these are not identified serovars in the source material.
Know More
  • Human leptospirosis caused by L. icterohaemorrhagiae is called Weil's disease.
  • Organisms can survive in water for up to 3 months.
  • Dark-field microscopy is used to identify spirochaetes.
  • Silver stains used include Levaditi and Warthin-Starry.

posts.post_title: Listeriosis (Circling Disease) is caused by…
posts.post_content: Listeriosis (Circling Disease) is caused by which organism?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Listeria monocytogenes

Listeriosis is caused by Listeria monocytogenes, a Gram-positive intracellular rod.

Correct Option Explanation

Surface proteins called internalins bind host E-cadherins, allowing the organism to invade epithelial cells and spread via the trigeminal nerve.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae is wrong — this causes Swine Erysipelas, a different septicaemic disease.
  • Corynebacterium pyogenes is wrong — this causes suppurative infections and summer mastitis, not encephalitis.
  • Actinobacillus lignieresi is wrong — this causes wooden tongue, unrelated to Listeria encephalitis.
Know More
  • Clinical encephalitis produces head tilt and 'circling'.
  • Abortion occurs typically in the last trimester.
  • Systemic form shows characteristic focal liver necrosis.
  • Organisms can be excreted in faeces even without disease.

posts.post_title: Brucellosis in cattle typically causes abort…
posts.post_content: Brucellosis in cattle typically causes abortion at which stage of gestation?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 7th and 8th months

In cattle, Brucella abortus infection typically causes abortion in the 7th and 8th months of gestation.

Correct Option Explanation

The organism has a special affinity for the chorio-allantoic trophoblast due to the presence of erythritol in placental tissue.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 2nd and 3rd months is wrong — this timing applies to pigs infected with Brucella suis.
  • 4th and 7th months is wrong — this range is associated with Campylobacter foetus venerealis abortion in cattle, not brucellosis.
  • 50 days of gestation is wrong — this timing is described for canine brucellosis (B. canis).
Know More
  • Bulls are relatively resistant to clinical brucellosis.
  • Human brucellosis is called 'Undulant fever' or Malta fever.
  • Brucella survives inside macrophages by preventing phagosome-lysosome fusion.
  • Horses show 'poll evil' and 'fistulous withers' from B. abortus plus Actinomyces bovis.

posts.post_title: Swine Erysipelas is characterized by which c…
posts.post_content: Swine Erysipelas is characterized by which classic skin lesion pattern?

_aimcq_options.text: Vesicles on the snout and coronary band
Papules restricted to the ventral abdomen
Nodular skin lesions with sulphur granules

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Rhomboid-shaped erythematous 'Diamond skin' lesions

Swine Erysipelas, caused by Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae, classically shows rhomboid 'Diamond skin' erythematous lesions.

Correct Option Explanation

Bacterial toxin injures vessel walls, causing skin erythema and, in chronic cases, vegetative endocarditis of the mitral valve.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Vesicles on snout/coronary band is wrong — this describes Vesicular Exanthema or FMD-type disease, not erysipelas.
  • Papules on ventral abdomen is wrong — this describes Swine pox, an unrelated viral disease.
  • Sulphur granule nodules is wrong — this describes Actinomycosis/Actinobacillosis, bacterial granulomas.
Know More
  • Erysipelothrix causes 'Erysipeloid' in humans.
  • Young pigs aged 3–6 months are most susceptible.
  • Chronic form shows vegetative valvular endocarditis.
  • Also affects sheep, cattle and birds.

posts.post_title: Ovine Caseous Lymphadenitis is caused by whi…
posts.post_content: Ovine Caseous Lymphadenitis is caused by which organism, showing which characteristic cut-surface appearance?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Corynebacterium pseudotuberculosis; onion-like concentric lamination

Caseous Lymphadenitis of sheep and goats is caused by Corynebacterium pseudotuberculosis (C. ovis).

Correct Option Explanation

Abscesses show an onion-like, concentrically laminated mass on cross-section, alternating fibrous capsule with greenish caseous material.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Listeria; miliary abscesses is wrong — Listeria causes encephalitis and hepatic necrosis, not this laminated abscess pattern.
  • Mycoplasma mycoides; marbled appearance is wrong — 'marbling' describes Contagious Bovine Pleuropneumonia lung lesions.
  • Nocardia asteroides; filamentous is wrong — Nocardia causes purulent necrotizing pulmonary lesions, not the onion-ring abscess.
Know More
  • Also called pseudotuberculosis of sheep and goats.
  • Abscesses rupture producing thick, green pus.
  • Calcification occurs without giant cell formation.
  • Diagnosis includes indirect haemagglutination and ELISA.

posts.post_title: Campylobacter foetus subspecies venerealis c…
posts.post_content: Campylobacter foetus subspecies venerealis causes which reproductive disease pattern in cattle?

_aimcq_options.text: Infertility, prolonged oestrus cycle and abortion at 4-7 months, spread by coitus
Abortion at 7-8 months, spread by ingestion of placenta
Orchitis in bulls with skeletal localisation
Mummification and maceration of the foetus by oral transmission

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Infertility, prolonged oestrus cycle and abortion at 4-7 months, spread by coitus

C. foetus venerealis causes venereal disease in cattle with infertility, prolonged oestrus and abortion at 4–7 months, spread by coitus or AI.

Correct Option Explanation

The organism shows cyclical antigenic variation, evading host IgA/IgG immunity in cervico-vaginal mucus and allowing persistent infection.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Abortion at 7–8 months by ingestion is wrong — this pattern describes Brucella abortus, not Campylobacter venerealis.
  • Orchitis with skeletal localisation is wrong — this is a feature of Brucella suis infection in pigs.
  • Mummification via oral transmission is wrong — this describes C. foetus subsp. foetus infection in sheep, not the venereal form in cattle.
Know More
  • Bulls act as symptomless carriers.
  • IgA in cervico-vaginal mucus helps eliminate the organism.
  • C. foetus subsp. foetus in sheep causes late abortion via the oral route.
  • C. jejuni causes diarrhoea and mastitis in various animals.

posts.post_title: Oedema Disease of swine is caused by a toxin…
posts.post_content: Oedema Disease of swine is caused by a toxin from Escherichia coli that is structurally similar to which toxin?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Shiga-like toxin

Oedema Disease of swine, also called enterotoxaemic colibacillosis, is caused by a Shiga-like toxin from E. coli.

Correct Option Explanation

This toxin causes necrotising arteritis and oedema of the stomach wall and colon, with mortality approaching 100%.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Botulinum toxin is wrong — this is a Clostridium botulinum neurotoxin, unrelated to E. coli oedema disease.
  • Tetanospasmin is wrong — this is the Clostridium tetani neurotoxin, causing spastic paralysis, not oedema.
  • Alpha toxin of Cl. perfringens is wrong — this causes haemolysis and helps bacterial spread, unrelated to this E. coli toxin.
Know More
  • Morbidity is around 35% though mortality is near 100%.
  • Clinical signs include incoordination and limb paralysis.
  • Enterotoxic colibacillosis mainly affects piglets in the first week of life.
  • Septicaemic colibacillosis causes polyserositis without diarrhoea.

posts.post_title: Contagious Bovine Pleuropneumonia produces a…
posts.post_content: Contagious Bovine Pleuropneumonia produces a characteristic gross lung lesion called:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 'Marbling' of the lung with sequestration

Contagious Bovine Pleuropneumonia, caused by Mycoplasma mycoides, produces a 'marbled' lung appearance with sequestration.

Correct Option Explanation

Thickened interlobular septa from fibrinous exudate create the marbled pattern, and necrotic areas wall off into a fibrous sequestrum.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 'Turkey egg' kidney is wrong — this petechial kidney pattern is described in Swine Fever.
  • 'Tigroid heart' is wrong — this myocardial lesion is characteristic of FMD in calves.
  • 'Wooden tongue' is wrong — this describes lingual fibrosis in Actinobacillosis.
Know More
  • Carrier animals in a herd are called 'lungers'.
  • Lesions are usually limited to one lung.
  • Contagious Caprine Pleuropneumonia, unlike the bovine form, shows minimal marbling.
  • The organism is classified as a pleuropneumonia-like organism (PPLO).

posts.post_title: Anaplasmosis (Gall Sickness) in cattle is ch…
posts.post_content: Anaplasmosis (Gall Sickness) in cattle is characterized by severe anaemia and icterus but classically WITHOUT which finding?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Haemoglobinuria

Anaplasmosis causes severe anaemia and icterus without haemoglobinuria, distinguishing it from haemolytic diseases like Babesiosis.

Correct Option Explanation

Anaplasma marginale infects erythrocytes, which are then removed by phagocytosis in the spleen rather than undergoing intravascular haemolysis.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Fever is wrong — high fever is a typical feature of anaplasmosis, not something the disease lacks.
  • Weakness is wrong — extreme weakness is a characteristic clinical sign of anaplasmosis.
  • Icterus is wrong — icterus is a defining clinical feature of the disease, not something it lacks.
Know More
  • Transmission occurs via ticks, biting flies or mosquitoes.
  • Young animals are relatively resistant to clinical disease.
  • Haematology shows anisocytosis and punctate basophilia.
  • Causative agents include Anaplasma marginale and A. centrale.

posts.post_title: Q Fever, a febrile disease of slaughterhouse…
posts.post_content: Q Fever, a febrile disease of slaughterhouse workers, is caused by which organism?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Coxiella burnetii

Q Fever is caused by Coxiella burnetii (also called Rickettsia burnetii), a minute pleomorphic intracellular rod.

Correct Option Explanation

Humans acquire it by contact with freshly slaughtered cattle/sheep or by consuming raw milk; the organism concentrates heavily in the placenta.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Chlamydia psittaci is wrong — this causes diseases like enzootic abortion of ewes and sporadic bovine encephalomyelitis, not Q fever.
  • Ehrlichia phagocytophilia is wrong — this causes tick-borne fever in sheep and cattle, a different rickettsial disease.
  • Rickettsia rickettsii is not identified in this text as the Q fever agent.
Know More
  • Q fever was first reported in Queensland, Australia.
  • Clinical signs in cattle are usually inapparent or mild.
  • In humans, it can cause interstitial pneumonia and granulomas.
  • Diagnosis uses guinea pig inoculation and Giemsa-Machiavello staining.

posts.post_title: Potomac Horse Fever (Equine Monocytic Ehrlic…
posts.post_content: Potomac Horse Fever (Equine Monocytic Ehrlichiosis) is caused by which organism?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Ehrlichia risticii

Potomac Horse Fever is caused by Ehrlichia risticii, first reported at the Potomac River, USA in 1979.

Correct Option Explanation

It causes biphasic fever, colic and diarrhoea, with the organism visible in circulating monocytes; mortality is about 30%.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Ehrlichia canis is wrong — this causes Canine Ehrlichiosis, transmitted by Rhipicephalus sanguineus ticks.
  • Ehrlichia equi is wrong — this causes a separate disease, Equine Ehrlichiosis, with oedema of legs and orchitis.
  • Ehrlichia phagocytophilia is wrong — this causes tick-borne fever of sheep and cattle, not Potomac Horse Fever.
Know More
  • Transmission occurs seasonally in summer months via an arthropod vector.
  • No single diagnostic gross lesion exists; haemorrhages occur in caecum and colon.
  • Canine ehrlichiosis shows 'mulberry bodies' or morulae within monocytes.
  • Equine ehrlichiosis produces petechiae, oedema and jaundice.

posts.post_title: Sporadic Bovine Encephalomyelitis in young c…
posts.post_content: Sporadic Bovine Encephalomyelitis in young calves is caused by which organism?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Chlamydia psittaci

Sporadic Bovine Encephalomyelitis is caused by Chlamydia psittaci, mainly affecting young calves.

Correct Option Explanation

Elementary bodies known as Levinthal-Colle-Lillie (LCL) bodies are seen in mononuclear cells of serosal exudate and CNS tissue.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Listeria monocytogenes is wrong — this causes Listeriosis with circling disease, a different bacterial encephalitis.
  • Coxiella burnetii is wrong — this causes Q Fever, not sporadic bovine encephalomyelitis.
  • Ehrlichia equi is wrong — this causes Equine Ehrlichiosis, unrelated to bovine encephalomyelitis.
Know More
  • Death typically occurs within 5–7 days of onset.
  • Gross lesions include serofibrinous peritonitis over the omentum.
  • The same organism causes Enzootic Abortion of Ewes.
  • Polyarthritis in calves is another Chlamydia psittaci-associated disease.

posts.post_title: Enzootic Abortion of Ewes is caused by which…
posts.post_content: Enzootic Abortion of Ewes is caused by which organism and shows which placental change?

_aimcq_options.text: Chlamydia psittaci; placentitis with dark red cotyledons

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Chlamydia psittaci; placentitis with dark red cotyledons

Enzootic Abortion of Ewes is caused by Chlamydia psittaci, producing placentitis with dark red cotyledons.

Correct Option Explanation
