posts.post_title: Which equine disease is characterized by ant…
posts.post_content: Which equine disease is characterized by antigenic drift so extreme that circulating antibody never fully neutralises the virus, leading to periodic febrile relapses over the horse's life?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:

posts.post_title: Which virus family causes Aujeszky's disease…
posts.post_content: Which virus family causes Aujeszky's disease and is also responsible for latency in host tissue with possible reactivation?

posts.post_title: Feline Infectious Peritonitis's immune-media…

posts.post_title: Which parasite characteristically obstructs…
posts.post_content: Which parasite characteristically obstructs the right ventricle and pulmonary artery of dogs, exemplifying mechanical vascular interference by helminths?

posts.post_title: According to helminth classification of host…
posts.post_content: According to helminth classification of host damage mechanisms, which effect is exemplified by Spirocerca lupi predisposing to oesophageal neoplasia?

posts.post_title: Within the phylum Apicomplexa, which genus h…
posts.post_content: Within the phylum Apicomplexa, which genus has a direct life cycle with an encysted extra-host form, unlike Babesia or Toxoplasma which need an intermediate host?

  • Babesia is wrong — this genus requires ticks as an intermediate host, an indirect life cycle.

posts.post_title: Which subphylum of protozoa includes Trypano…
posts.post_content: Which subphylum of protozoa includes Trypanosoma and Giardia, characterized by trophozoites bearing one or more flagella?

Mastigophora includes flagellated protozoa such as Trypanosoma and Giardia.

  • Leishmania is an example of an intracellular Mastigophoran parasite.

posts.post_title: Ochratoxicosis, also called 'Mouldy Nephrosi…
posts.post_content: Ochratoxicosis, also called 'Mouldy Nephrosis' of swine, primarily damages which part of the kidney?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Proximal convoluted tubule

Ochratoxin A is particularly toxic to the proximal convoluted tubule of the kidney in pigs.

Produced by Penicillium viridicatum and Aspergillus ochraceus, it causes polydipsia, polyuria and retarded growth, with tubular epithelial pyknosis and necrosis.

  • Glomerulus only is wrong — while peritubular fibrosis can eventually involve glomeruli, the primary target is the proximal tubule.

  • It is also known as citrinin toxicity when caused by a related mycotoxin.

posts.post_title: Lupinosis, caused by the mycotoxin phomopsin…
posts.post_content: Lupinosis, caused by the mycotoxin phomopsin, mainly affects which species when fed lupine forage?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Sheep

Lupinosis is usually seen in sheep, resulting from greater use of lupine forage crops contaminated with the fungus Phomopsis leptostromiformis.

Correct Option Explanation

Clinical signs include anorexia, jaundice and death within days, with liver enlargement, focal necrosis and eventual scarring.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Cats is wrong — cats are not the primary species described for lupinosis; this is a forage-related disease of grazing livestock.
  • Poultry is wrong — poultry are not identified as commonly affected by lupinosis in this text.
  • Horses is wrong — while horses (and cattle, pigs) have been reported affected, sheep are the species usually affected.

  • The disease also occurs in New Zealand, Australia, Europe and South Africa.
  • Serum liver enzymes (SGOT, LDH, ALP) are elevated.
  • Photosensitization may accompany lupinosis.

posts.post_title: Trichothecene mycotoxins (T-2 toxin, DAS) ex…
posts.post_content: Trichothecene mycotoxins (T-2 toxin, DAS) exert their cytotoxic effect mainly by which mechanism?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Potent inhibition of protein synthesis

Trichothecenes such as T-2 toxin and DAS are potent inhibitors of protein synthesis, accounting for their cytotoxicity.

Correct Option Explanation

They cause necrosis of skin and mucous membranes on contact, along with necrosis of lymphoid organs, bone marrow and gastrointestinal epithelium.

  • DNA cross-linking is wrong — this is not the mechanism described for trichothecene toxicity in this text.
  • Acetylcholine blockade is wrong — this describes botulinum toxin action, not trichothecene mycotoxins.
  • Uncoupling oxidative phosphorylation is wrong — this is not the mechanism attributed to trichothecenes here.
Know More
  • Vomitoxin (DON) causes anorexia and vomiting, especially in pigs.
  • Satratoxin causes stachybotryotoxicosis from mouldy straw/hay.
  • In cattle, a T-2 related condition is called 'mouldy corn poisoning' with extensive haemorrhage.
  • Toxin production increases with cool-temperature storage.

posts.post_title: Equine Leukoencephalomalacia ('Mouldy Corn P…
posts.post_content: Equine Leukoencephalomalacia ('Mouldy Corn Poisoning') produces which characteristic gross brain lesion in horses?

_aimcq_options.text: Softening and liquefactive necrosis of cerebral white matter

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Softening and liquefactive necrosis of cerebral white matter

Equine Leukoencephalomalacia produces softening and liquefactive necrosis chiefly of the cerebral white matter in horses and donkeys.

Correct Option Explanation

Affected horses become drowsy, circle, and develop paralysis, with minimal cellular inflammatory reaction accompanying the oedema and congestion.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Cerebellar spongiform vacuolation is wrong — this pattern describes prion diseases like BSE/Scrapie, not mouldy corn poisoning.
  • Non-suppurative encephalitis with cuffing is wrong — this inflammatory pattern is typical of viral encephalitides, not the largely non-inflammatory necrosis of leukoencephalomalacia.
  • Pontine haemorrhages only is wrong — the lesion is chiefly cerebral white matter liquefactive necrosis, not isolated pontine bleeding.
Know More
  • The condition results from feeding mouldy corn contaminated with various moulds.
  • Term 'mouldy corn poisoning' covers several distinct syndromes.
  • Little cellular inflammatory reaction accompanies the necrosis.
  • Affected horses may show drowsiness before paralysis develops.

posts.post_title: Dallis Grass Poisoning, caused by Claviceps…
posts.post_content: Dallis Grass Poisoning, caused by Claviceps paspli, primarily produces which type of clinical sign?

_aimcq_options.text: Gangrene of the limbs and tail

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Nervous hyperirritability and muscular incoordination

Dallis Grass Poisoning primarily produces nervous hyperirritability, excitability and muscular incoordination in cattle, sheep and horses.

Correct Option Explanation

It is caused by a smaller, brownish sclerotium of Claviceps paspali growing on Dallis grass, distinct from Claviceps purpurea ergot.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Gangrene of limbs/tail is wrong — this describes classic ergotism from Claviceps purpurea, not Dallis grass poisoning.
  • Hepatic photosensitization is wrong — this describes facial eczema from sporidesmin, a different mycotoxicosis.
  • Nephrotoxic polyuria is wrong — this describes ochratoxicosis, not Dallis grass poisoning.
Know More
  • Most animals recover with a change in feed.
  • Gross lesions are few, and microscopic studies are limited.
  • The ergot of C. paspali is smaller than that of C. purpurea.
  • It occurs in the United States on Dallis grass pastures.

posts.post_title: In Canine Ehrlichiosis, the granular intrace…
posts.post_content: In Canine Ehrlichiosis, the granular intracellular forms of Ehrlichia canis seen as clusters within monocytes are called:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Mulberry bodies (morulae)

Mulberry bodies, or morulae, are granular intracellular forms of Ehrlichia canis found within monocytes.

Correct Option Explanation

Three intracellular forms of E. canis are recognised: initial bodies, morulae (mulberry bodies), and elementary bodies.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Negri bodies is wrong — these are rabies viral inclusions in neurons, unrelated to Ehrlichia.
  • Koch's blue bodies is wrong — these are Theileria schizonts in lymphocytes, a different rickettsial-like organism.
  • Babes nodules is wrong — these are microglial nodules seen in rabies, unrelated to Ehrlichia canis.
Know More
  • Transmission occurs via the tick Rhipicephalus sanguineus.
  • Clinical signs include recurrent fever and thrombocytopenia.
  • Diagnosis uses indirect fluorescent antibody test.
  • Bone marrow hypoplasia is a described lesion.

posts.post_title: Gluten enteropathy, associated with villus a…
posts.post_content: Gluten enteropathy, associated with villus atrophy and intraepithelial lymphocytic infiltration, has been identified in which dog breed?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Irish Setters

Gluten enteropathy, similar to the human condition, has been identified in Irish Setters.

Correct Option Explanation

It is characterized by villus atrophy and intraepithelial lymphocytic infiltration, analogous to wheat-gluten enteropathy in humans.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Doberman Pinschers is wrong — this breed is not identified in this text as prone to gluten enteropathy.
  • German Shepherds is wrong — this breed is not the one specifically named for gluten enteropathy here.
  • Labrador Retrievers is wrong — this breed is not the one specifically named for gluten enteropathy in this text.
Know More
  • No specific carbohydrate deficiency state exists in most animals.
  • Dogs and cats do not require a dietary carbohydrate source.
  • Reduced carbohydrate availability precipitates ketosis in cattle.
  • Reduced carbohydrate contributes to pregnancy toxaemia in sheep/cattle.

posts.post_title: Protein-deficient diets in young growing ani…
posts.post_content: Protein-deficient diets in young growing animals cause failure to grow primarily through which mechanism affecting bone?

_aimcq_options.text: Cessation of cell proliferation of epiphyseal cartilage with reduced osteoblastic activity

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Cessation of cell proliferation of epiphyseal cartilage with reduced osteoblastic activity

Protein deficiency causes cessation of epiphyseal cartilage cell proliferation and reduced osteoblastic activity, halting normal bone growth.

Correct Option Explanation

Other effects include failure of collagen formation, atrophy of endocrine glands and lymphoid tissue, fatty liver, anaemia and hypoproteinaemic oedema.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Excess mineralisation is wrong — protein deficiency impairs growth through reduced cell proliferation, not excess mineralisation.
  • Direct bacterial infection is wrong — this is not the mechanism of protein-deficiency-related growth failure described.
  • Parathyroid hormone overproduction is wrong — this is not implicated in the described protein-deficiency pathology.
Know More
  • Effects are complicated by superimposed infections.
  • Atrophy of testicle, ovary and thymus can occur.
  • Hypoproteinaemia and oedema are described consequences.
  • Lesions are generally non-specific.

posts.post_title: Essential fatty acid/fat deficiency in domes…
posts.post_content: Essential fatty acid/fat deficiency in domestic animals is rare but, when it occurs, causes which skin change progression?

_aimcq_options.text: Dryness, followed by erythema, alopecia, scaling and ulceration
Excess sebum production with no hair loss

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Dryness, followed by erythema, alopecia, scaling and ulceration

Fat/essential fatty acid deficiency causes a skin change progression of dryness, then erythema, alopecia, scaling and ulceration.

Correct Option Explanation

Microscopically, epidermal thickening with hyperkeratosis occurs, and hair follicles become hypercellular and plugged with keratin.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Immediate ulceration is wrong — the described progression starts with dryness and erythema before reaching ulceration.
  • Hyperpigmentation only is wrong — this is not the described skin change pattern for fat deficiency.
  • Excess sebum, no hair loss is wrong — the described pathology specifically includes alopecia (hair loss), not excess sebum without hair loss.
Know More
  • Deficiency occurs when fat absorption is impaired in biliary or pancreatic disease.
  • In cats, fatty change of liver and kidney develops with adrenal mineralisation.
  • True dietary deficiency of essential fatty acids is rare in domestic animals.
  • Dietary fat supplementation can improve certain skin disorders.

posts.post_title: Which Corynebacterium species causes pyelone…
posts.post_content: Which Corynebacterium species causes pyelonephritis, ureteritis and haemorrhagic cystitis specifically in cows?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Corynebacterium renale

Corynebacterium renale causes pyelonephritis, ureteritis and haemorrhagic cystitis in cows.

Correct Option Explanation

This organism is distinct from other Corynebacteria that cause different disease patterns in different hosts across veterinary species.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • C. pyogenes (Actinomyces pyogenes) is wrong — this causes general suppurative infections and summer mastitis in cattle, not specifically pyelonephritis.
  • C. pseudotuberculosis is wrong — this causes caseous lymphadenitis in sheep and goats, a different disease.
  • C. equi (Rhodococcus equi) is wrong — this causes pneumonia in foals, not bovine urinary tract disease.
Know More
  • C. diphtheriae causes disease in humans.
  • C. bovis and C. suis cause pyelonephritis and cystitis in pigs.
  • C. ulcerans causes wound infections and abscesses.
  • C. pyogenes is now also classified as Actinomyces pyogenes.

posts.post_title: At progressively higher levels, bacterial LP…
posts.post_content: At progressively higher levels, bacterial LPS (endotoxin) ultimately causes which severe systemic outcome via disseminated coagulation?

_aimcq_options.text: Septic/endotoxic shock with disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)
Simple fever with no vascular effect

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Septic/endotoxic shock with disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)

At high levels, LPS induces septic/endotoxic shock via systemic vasodilation, reduced cardiac output and activation of coagulation, causing DIC.

Correct Option Explanation

At lower levels, LPS instead activates macrophages and complement to help eliminate bacteria, showing a dose-dependent spectrum of effects.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Localized abscess formation is wrong — this is a different, more localized bacterial response pattern, not the systemic LPS cascade.
  • Chronic granuloma formation is wrong — this is a cell-mediated response to organisms like Mycobacteria, not the acute LPS cascade.
  • Simple fever with no vascular effect is wrong — high-dose LPS produces profound vascular and coagulation effects, not just fever.
Know More
  • LPS-protein complexes bind CD14 on leukocytes and endothelial cells.
  • IL-1 and TNF are released following macrophage activation.
  • LPS consists of lipid A joined to a core sugar and O antigen chain.
  • O antigen is used for bacterial serotyping.

posts.post_title: In rabbits, hepatic coccidiosis caused by Ei…
posts.post_content: In rabbits, hepatic coccidiosis caused by Eimeria stiedae produces liver nodules resembling which type of hyperplastic change?

_aimcq_options.text: Fibrous cirrhotic nodules without epithelial change

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Adenomatous hyperplasia of biliary epithelium

Eimeria stiedae causes intrahepatic bile duct coccidiosis with proliferation of biliary epithelium resembling adenomatous hyperplasia.

Correct Option Explanation

Early lesions show destruction of biliary epithelium, while longer-course disease shows epithelial proliferation into papillary folds.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Squamous metaplasia is wrong — this epithelial change is characteristic of vitamin A deficiency, not coccidial bile duct disease.
  • Granulomatous caseous necrosis is wrong — this pattern is more typical of tuberculosis, not E. stiedae hepatic coccidiosis.
  • Fibrous cirrhotic nodules without epithelial change is wrong — the hallmark here is specifically epithelial proliferation, not simple fibrosis.
Know More
  • Liver is studded with round, grey nodules containing large numbers of coccidia.
  • E. stiedae specifically affects the intrahepatic bile duct epithelium.
  • The oocyst is the resistant stage passed in faeces.
  • Coccidiosis in birds can show mortality of 90–100%.

posts.post_title: In Theileriosis, infected lymphoblasts proli…
posts.post_content: In Theileriosis, infected lymphoblasts proliferate rapidly because the parasite triggers production of which cytokine and its receptor?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Interleukin-2 (IL-2) and its receptor

Theileria schizonts trigger production of Interleukin-2 (IL-2) and its receptor, driving rapid clonal expansion of infected lymphoblasts.

Correct Option Explanation

Since the parasite divides along with the host cell, this produces overwhelming infection in most cattle, though cytotoxic CD8+ cells can kill infected lymphoblasts in survivors.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • TNF-alpha only is wrong — while TNF is relevant in other bacterial contexts (e.g., LPS, tuberculosis), IL-2 is specifically named in Theileria's lymphoproliferative mechanism.
  • IL-10 only is wrong — IL-10 is described in the context of Mycobacterium tuberculosis suppressing T-cell proliferation, not Theileria.
  • Interferon gamma only is wrong — this is not the cytokine specifically implicated in Theileria's lymphoblast proliferation mechanism.
Know More
  • The parasite can invade both T cells and B cells.
  • Koch's blue bodies are the pathognomonic schizont stage.
  • T. annulata is the species seen in India.
  • Cytotoxic CD8+ cells kill infected lymphoblasts in immune survivors.

posts.post_title: Anaplasma marginale and A. centrale can be d…
posts.post_content: Anaplasma marginale and A. centrale can be differentiated by their position within the erythrocyte; A. marginale is typically located:

_aimcq_options.text: At the periphery of the erythrocyte
At the exact centre of the erythrocyte

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: At the periphery of the erythrocyte

Anaplasma marginale is a coccoid form typically seen at the periphery of the erythrocyte and is the more virulent species.

Correct Option Explanation

In contrast, A. centrale is usually seen toward the centre of the cell and causes a milder disease.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Exact centre is wrong — this position describes A. centrale, the milder species, not A. marginale.
  • Outside erythrocyte in plasma is wrong — Anaplasma organisms are intraerythrocytic, not free in plasma.
  • Within erythrocyte nucleus is wrong — mature mammalian erythrocytes lack a nucleus, and Anaplasma resides in the cytoplasm.
Know More
  • Anaplasmosis is also called Gall Sickness.
  • No haemoglobinuria occurs since infected cells are removed by splenic phagocytosis.
  • Transmission occurs by ticks, biting flies or mosquitoes.
  • Complement fixation and FAT are used diagnostically.

posts.post_title: Cyanide (HCN) toxicity from cyanogenic plant…
posts.post_content: Cyanide (HCN) toxicity from cyanogenic plant poisoning causes death mainly through which mechanism?

_aimcq_options.text: Cytotoxic anoxia via inhibition of cytochrome oxidase

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Cytotoxic anoxia via inhibition of cytochrome oxidase

Cyanide causes cytotoxic anoxia through its high affinity for cytochrome oxidase, blocking cellular oxygen utilisation.

Correct Option Explanation

This causes sudden death, often within 10–25 minutes of ingesting large amounts of cyanogenic plant material, without premonitory signs.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Corrosive gastric damage is wrong — cyanide toxicity is a biochemical (cytotoxic) mechanism, not a direct caustic/corrosive injury.
  • Methaemoglobin formation is wrong — this describes the mechanism of nitrite poisoning, not cyanide.
  • Acetylcholinesterase inhibition is wrong — this describes the mechanism of organophosphate insecticide poisoning, not cyanide.
Know More
  • Cattle and buffaloes are most susceptible among livestock.
  • Monogastric animals are relatively resistant due to gastric acid destroying glycosides.
  • Sorghum fodder is a common source of cyanide poisoning in India.
  • Blood remains bright red and unclotted at postmortem.

posts.post_title: Strychnine poisoning produces tonic seizures…
posts.post_content: Strychnine poisoning produces tonic seizures and a 'saw horse' stance by antagonising which receptor?

_aimcq_options.text: Glycine receptors in the spinal cord

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Glycine receptors in the spinal cord

Strychnine is a competitive glycine receptor antagonist, blocking inhibitory neurotransmission at Renshaw cells in the spinal cord.

Correct Option Explanation

This removes normal inhibitory control of motor reflexes, causing extensor rigidity, opisthotonus and the classic 'saw horse' stance.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Acetylcholine receptors is wrong — cholinergic receptor effects are characteristic of organophosphate poisoning, not strychnine.
  • GABA receptors is wrong — GABA receptor antagonism is the mechanism of organochlorine cyclodiene insecticides, not strychnine.
  • Dopamine receptors is wrong — dopaminergic pathways are not the site of strychnine's toxic action.
Know More
  • Onset occurs within 10 minutes to 2 hours of ingestion.
  • Animals remain conscious until near death.
  • Death results from asphyxia due to respiratory muscle paralysis.
  • Poisoning is often from bait intended for foxes or rodents.

posts.post_title: Acute oxalate poisoning in livestock produce…
posts.post_content: Acute oxalate poisoning in livestock produces acute hypocalcaemia mainly through which mechanism?

_aimcq_options.text: Absorbed soluble oxalates chelate blood calcium
Renal excretion of calcium is increased directly by oxalate

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Absorbed soluble oxalates chelate blood calcium

In oxalate poisoning, absorbed soluble oxalates chelate blood calcium directly, causing acute hypocalcaemia.

Correct Option Explanation

Excess ingestion overwhelms the digestive tract's capacity to convert oxalates to insoluble calcium oxalate, allowing systemic absorption and calcium chelation.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Parathyroid destruction is wrong — the mechanism described is direct chemical chelation of calcium, not glandular destruction.
  • Vitamin D receptor blockade is wrong — this is not the mechanism of oxalate-induced hypocalcaemia described.
  • Increased renal calcium excretion is wrong — the primary described mechanism is chelation of blood calcium by absorbed oxalate, not renal loss.
Know More
  • Calcium oxalate crystals can accumulate in renal tubules causing damage.
  • Ruminants tolerate more oxalate than monogastrics due to rumen conversion.
  • Plants must generally contain over 10% oxalic acid (dry weight) to cause toxicity.
  • Clinical signs include salivation, incoordination and coma.

posts.post_title: Organophosphorus insecticides exert toxicity…
posts.post_content: Organophosphorus insecticides exert toxicity mainly by inhibiting which enzyme?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Acetylcholinesterase

Organophosphorus insecticides inhibit acetylcholinesterase (AChE), causing accumulation of acetylcholine at nerve endings.

Correct Option Explanation

Death typically occurs when brain AChE is inhibited by about 95%, producing muscarinic, nicotinic and central nervous system symptoms.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Cytochrome oxidase is wrong — this enzyme is the target of cyanide toxicity, not organophosphates.
  • Monoamine oxidase is wrong — this enzyme is unrelated to the described organophosphate mechanism.
  • Glutathione peroxidase is wrong — this selenium-dependent enzyme relates to antioxidant defence, not organophosphate toxicity.
Know More
  • Muscarinic signs include bronchoconstriction, salivation and diarrhoea.
  • Nicotinic signs include muscle twitching and fasciculations.
  • Delayed neuropathy is linked to inhibition of neurotoxic esterases (NTE).
  • Death results from respiratory failure/asphyxia.

posts.post_title: DDT, an organochlorine insecticide, exerts i…
posts.post_content: DDT, an organochlorine insecticide, exerts its neurotoxic effect primarily by acting on which cellular structure?

_aimcq_options.text: Sodium channels of the nerve membrane

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Sodium channels of the nerve membrane

DDT acts on sodium channels of the nerve membrane, inactivating sodium channel closure and disrupting normal nerve conduction.

Correct Option Explanation

It also inhibits Na+-K+ and Ca2+-Mg2+ ATPases and calmodulin-Ca2+ binding, promoting neurotransmitter release.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • GABA-gated chloride channels is wrong — this is the mechanism of cyclodiene compounds and lindane, not DDT specifically.
  • Acetylcholinesterase enzyme is wrong — this enzyme is the target of organophosphate insecticides, not organochlorines like DDT.
  • Nicotinic receptors is wrong — this is not DDT's primary mechanism; DDT targets sodium channels.
Know More
  • Cyclodienes act on chloride channels by antagonising GABA receptors.
  • Chronic DDT/methoxychlor toxicity causes centrilobular hepatic necrosis.
  • DDT is metabolised to the persistent metabolite DDE.
  • Organochlorines other than methoxychlor are stored in body fat.

posts.post_title: Rift Valley Fever, first reported in Kenya i…
posts.post_content: Rift Valley Fever, first reported in Kenya in 1912, is transmitted mainly by which vector?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Culicine mosquitoes

Rift Valley Fever is transmitted mainly by culicine mosquitoes, causing heavy mortality in young lambs and calves and abortion in pregnant ewes/cows.

Correct Option Explanation

The most constant and characteristic lesions occur in the liver, which is grossly enlarged with foci of necrosis around central veins and intranuclear inclusions.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Culicoides midges is wrong — these transmit Bluetongue and African Horse Sickness, not Rift Valley Fever.
  • Ixodid ticks is wrong — ticks are not the described vector for Rift Valley Fever; it is arthropod-borne via mosquitoes.
  • Tsetse flies is wrong — these transmit trypanosomiasis (e.g. Nagana), not Rift Valley Fever.
Know More
  • The disease has zoonotic importance, with humans developing a febrile illness.
  • In adult sheep, animals may be found dead without prior signs of illness.
  • Cattle disease appears as a 'storm of abortions'.
  • Diagnosis includes a serum neutralisation test using mice.

posts.post_title: Akabane Disease of cattle, caused by a bunya…
posts.post_content: Akabane Disease of cattle, caused by a bunyavirus, produces which characteristic congenital syndrome in calves?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Arthrogryposis and/or hydranencephaly

Akabane virus causes congenital arthrogryposis (fixed joints) and/or hydranencephaly in calves, lambs and kids, without illness in the dam.

Correct Option Explanation

Which defect predominates depends on fetal age at infection: arthrogryposis follows infection later in gestation (105–174 days), while hydranencephaly follows earlier infection (days 76–104).

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Cerebellar hypoplasia only is wrong — this specific lesion is more typical of BVD or Feline Panleucopenia, not Akabane disease.
  • Cleft palate and micro-ophthalmos is wrong — these are congenital anomalies linked to vitamin A deficiency, not Akabane virus.
  • Rickets with bowed limbs is wrong — this is a vitamin D deficiency lesion, unrelated to this viral congenital syndrome.
Know More
  • Transmission occurs via mosquitoes and midges.
  • Myositis in affected fetuses gives rise to the name 'Runt-Muscle Disease'.
  • The cow herself remains clinically unaffected during infection.
  • The disease has occurred in Japan, Australia, Israel and the Middle East.

posts.post_title: Feline Leukaemia Virus (FeLV) infection most…
posts.post_content: Feline Leukaemia Virus (FeLV) infection most commonly results in which malignancy in cats?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Malignant lymphoma

Malignant lymphoma, with or without leukaemia, is the most common malignancy resulting from FeLV infection in cats.

Correct Option Explanation

FeLV causes lymphoma through viral activation of cellular proto-oncogenes, with forms including thymic (young cats), alimentary (older cats) and multicentric lymphoma.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Osteosarcoma is wrong — this tumour type is more associated with Spirocerca lupi infection in dogs, not FeLV in cats.
  • Mammary adenocarcinoma is wrong — this is not the malignancy typically linked to FeLV infection.
  • Squamous cell carcinoma is wrong — this is not the characteristic FeLV-associated tumour described in this text.
Know More
  • About 60% of infected cats mount a self-limiting (regressive) infection.
  • Feline sarcoma virus, a defective FeLV mutant, causes fibrosarcoma using FeLV as a helper virus.
  • Myelosuppression syndrome causes anaemia and leukopaenia.
  • Diagnosis includes fluorescent antibody testing of blood smears.

posts.post_title: Bovine Leukaemia Virus (BLV), a C-type oncov…
posts.post_content: Bovine Leukaemia Virus (BLV), a C-type oncovirus, primarily infects which cell type, leading to lymphocytosis or lymphoma?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: B lymphocytes

Bovine Leukaemia Virus primarily infects B lymphocytes, causing either persistent lymphocytosis or generalized lymphoma in adult cattle.

Correct Option Explanation

Enzootic bovine lymphoma often involves mesenteric and pelvic lymph nodes, with myocardial invasion (especially the right atrium) potentially causing heart failure.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • T lymphocytes is wrong — this cell type is instead the target of FIV, a distinct feline lentivirus.
  • Neutrophils is wrong — neutrophils are not the target cell population for BLV-induced lymphoproliferation.
  • Erythroid precursor cells is wrong — these cells are not the primary target of BLV; BLV targets B lymphocytes.
Know More
  • BLV was first isolated in 1969.
  • An alimentary form usually involves the abomasal wall and associated lymph nodes.
  • BLV can also cause generalized lymphoma in sheep and goats.
  • Infection spreads horizontally between cattle.

posts.post_title: Feline Immunodeficiency Virus (FIV), a lenti…
posts.post_content: Feline Immunodeficiency Virus (FIV), a lentivirus similar to HIV, is transmitted primarily through which route?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Bites (via saliva)

FIV is shed mainly in saliva and is transmitted primarily through bites, explaining its higher incidence in free-roaming, aged male cats.

Correct Option Explanation

FIV is tropic for T lymphocytes, macrophages and astrocytes, and causes an initial acute phase followed by a long clinically latent period before immunodeficiency develops.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Transplacental transmission is wrong — bite transmission via saliva is the primary route described for FIV, not transplacental spread.
  • Respiratory droplets is wrong — this is not the transmission route emphasised for FIV in this text.
  • Ingestion of contaminated milk is wrong — this is not the primary described transmission route for FIV.
Know More
  • FIV was first isolated in 1987 in the United States.
  • FIV is less immunosuppressive in cats than HIV is in humans.
  • Opportunistic infections include toxoplasmosis and cryptococcosis in advanced disease.
  • Encephalitis with perivascular cuffing and glial nodules is a primary FIV lesion.

posts.post_title: Bovine Immunodeficiency Virus (BIV) is class…
posts.post_content: Bovine Immunodeficiency Virus (BIV) is classified alongside which other viruses as one of the three bovine retroviruses?

_aimcq_options.text: Bovine Leukaemia Virus and Bovine Spumavirus
Bovine Papular Stomatitis virus and Vaccinia virus

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Bovine Leukaemia Virus and Bovine Spumavirus

BIV is one of three bovine retroviruses, alongside Bovine Leukaemia Virus (a type C oncovirus) and Bovine Spumavirus (a foamy virus).

Correct Option Explanation

BIV was actually the first bovine retrovirus isolated, recovered from a Holstein cow with lymphocytosis, though it was not found to cause bovine leukaemia.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Rinderpest virus and BVD virus is wrong — these are a Morbillivirus and Pestivirus respectively, not retroviruses grouped with BIV.
  • IBR virus and Bovine Adenovirus is wrong — these are a herpesvirus and an adenovirus, not retroviruses.
  • Bovine Papular Stomatitis virus and Vaccinia virus is wrong — these are poxviruses, unrelated to the retrovirus classification of BIV.
Know More
  • BIV was the third lentivirus discovered, after EIA virus and visna-maedi virus.
  • Persistent BIV infection predisposes to effects of bovine leukaemia virus.
  • Clinical findings include lethargy, mastitis and pododermatitis.
  • Lymphocytic cuffing and meningitis occur in the brain of infected cattle.

posts.post_title: Clinically, poisoning by Organophosphate ins…
posts.post_content: Clinically, poisoning by Organophosphate insecticides (OPIs) can be differentiated from chlorinated hydrocarbon insecticides (CHIs) by which pupillary sign?

_aimcq_options.text: Miosis (constricted pupils) in OPI poisoning versus normal pupils in CHI poisoning
Mydriasis in OPI poisoning versus miosis in CHI poisoning

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Miosis (constricted pupils) in OPI poisoning versus normal pupils in CHI poisoning

OPI poisoning classically causes miosis (constricted pupils), whereas pupils remain normal in chlorinated hydrocarbon (CHI) poisoning.

Correct Option Explanation

Additional differentiators include watery saliva and hypothermia with straight-line running in OPI toxicity, versus frothy saliva, hyperthermia and circling in CHI toxicity.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Mydriasis in OPI, miosis in CHI is wrong — this reverses the actual pattern; OPIs cause miosis, not mydriasis.
  • Both cause identical mydriasis is wrong — the two toxidromes are clinically distinguishable, and OPI causes miosis, not mydriasis.
  • Neither affects pupil size is wrong — pupillary constriction (miosis) is a specific and useful diagnostic sign in OPI poisoning.
Know More
  • OPI-poisoned animals run in a straight direction; CHI-poisoned animals move in circles.
  • Abnormal posturing like opisthotonus is seen with CHI poisoning, not typically OPI.
  • OPIs inhibit acetylcholinesterase; CHIs act on sodium/chloride channels.
  • Both classes can produce hypersalivation, though the character of saliva differs.

posts.post_title: In Contagious Caprine Pleuropneumonia caused…
posts.post_content: In Contagious Caprine Pleuropneumonia caused by Mycoplasma species, the lung lesion differs from the bovine disease mainly by which feature?

_aimcq_options.text: Minimal marbling of the lung compared to the bovine form
Complete absence of any lung involvement
Formation of button ulcers in the lung

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Minimal marbling of the lung compared to the bovine form

Unlike Contagious Bovine Pleuropneumonia, the caprine form shows minimal marbling of the lung despite being caused by a related Mycoplasma organism.

Correct Option Explanation

Both diseases share a mycoplasmal aetiology, but the pathological pattern and severity of interlobular septal involvement differ notably between species.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Complete absence of lung involvement is wrong — the caprine disease does still involve the lungs, just with less marbling, not a total absence of pathology.
  • Button ulcers is wrong — this intestinal lesion pattern is associated with Swine Fever, unrelated to pleuropneumonia.
  • Cavitation with abscess is wrong — this is not the distinguishing feature described between caprine and bovine pleuropneumonia.
Know More
  • Contagious Bovine Pleuropneumonia is caused by Mycoplasma mycoides.
  • Carrier cattle in a herd are termed 'lungers'.
  • Sequestra can form in the bovine disease from walled-off necrotic lung tissue.
  • Both diseases are classified as mycoplasma-caused respiratory infections.

posts.post_title: Which fungal genus is responsible for causin…
posts.post_content: Which fungal genus is responsible for causing thrush (candidiasis), a yeast infection commonly affecting mucocutaneous surfaces?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Candida

Candida species (notably C. albicans) cause thrush (candidiasis), typically affecting mucocutaneous surfaces such as the oral cavity and crop.

Correct Option Explanation

Candidiasis is generally an opportunistic infection, occurring more readily in young, debilitated or immunocompromised animals, or after prolonged antibiotic use.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Cryptococcus is wrong — this yeast causes cryptococcosis, mainly affecting the respiratory tract and CNS, not classic mucocutaneous thrush.
  • Coccidioides is wrong — this fungus causes coccidioidomycosis, forming spherules in tissue, a deep systemic mycosis distinct from candidiasis.
  • Histoplasma is wrong — this fungus causes histoplasmosis, a systemic granulomatous disease, not superficial thrush.
Know More
  • Candida is part of normal mucosal flora that becomes pathogenic opportunistically.
  • Prolonged antibiotic therapy predisposes to candidiasis by disrupting normal flora.
  • Lesions show pseudohyphae and budding yeast forms.
  • Crop mycosis in birds is a recognised presentation of candidiasis.

posts.post_title: In the classification of helminth-induced ho…
posts.post_content: In the classification of helminth-induced host damage, hookworms like Bunostomum and Ancylostoma primarily damage the host through which mechanism?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Direct blood sucking causing anaemia

Hookworms such as Bunostomum and Ancylostoma primarily damage the host through direct blood sucking, causing progressive anaemia.

Correct Option Explanation

This blood-loss mechanism is distinct from mechanical obstruction (as with Dirofilaria) or oncogenic effects (as with Spirocerca lupi).

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Mechanical vascular obstruction is wrong — this mechanism is exemplified by Dirofilaria immitis, not hookworms.
  • Induction of neoplasia is wrong — this mechanism is exemplified by Spirocerca lupi, not hookworms.
  • Toxin-mediated paralysis is wrong — this is not a described mechanism for hookworm pathogenicity; blood loss is the key mechanism.
Know More
  • Over 2000 Bunostomum worms can be fatal in calves.
  • Ancylostoma caninum affects dogs and cats specifically.
  • Haemonchus contortus similarly causes anaemia via blood-sucking in the abomasum.
  • Severity of hookworm disease correlates with worm burden.

posts.post_title: Equine Viral Arteritis is caused by a Toga v…
posts.post_content: Equine Viral Arteritis is caused by a Toga virus that is now considered related to which other virus family, distinguishing it from other equine viral diseases?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Corona virus

Equine Viral Arteritis is caused by a Toga virus now considered related to Corona virus, distinguishing it from the other listed equine diseases.

Correct Option Explanation

This contrasts with Equine Influenza (Orthomyxovirus), African Horse Sickness (Orbivirus) and EIA (Lentivirus), each belonging to unrelated viral families.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Orthomyxovirus is wrong — this family includes Equine Influenza virus, not EVA.
  • Orbivirus is wrong — this family includes African Horse Sickness virus, not EVA.
  • Lentivirus is wrong — this family includes the Equine Infectious Anaemia virus, not EVA.
Know More
  • EVA was first reported in the USA in 1957.
  • Carrier stallions can shed EVA virus in semen for up to 2 years.
  • TGE and FIP viruses are also coronaviruses, unrelated taxonomically to EVA's original Togavirus classification.
  • Arterial media replacement by eosinophilic material is a key EVA lesion.

posts.post_title: Which zoonotic bacterial disease of cattle a…
posts.post_content: Which zoonotic bacterial disease of cattle and buffalo produces human infection termed 'Undulant Fever' or 'Malta Fever'?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Brucellosis

Brucellosis causes human infection known as 'Undulant Fever' or 'Malta Fever', typically acquired from infected animals or unpasteurised dairy products.

Correct Option Explanation

Brucella organisms survive inside macrophages by preventing phagosome-lysosome fusion, contributing to their chronic, relapsing nature in both animals and humans.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Leptospirosis is wrong — the human form of leptospirosis caused by L. icterohaemorrhagiae is called Weil's disease, not Malta Fever.
  • Anthrax is wrong — human cutaneous anthrax is called 'Malignant Carbuncle', not Undulant/Malta Fever.
  • Q Fever is wrong — this rickettsial disease causes a distinct febrile illness in humans, not termed Malta Fever.
Know More
  • Brucella abortus has affinity for placental erythritol.
  • Bulls are relatively resistant to clinical disease.
  • Cattle typically abort in the 7th–8th month of gestation.
  • Human infection often follows contact with infected animals or raw milk.

posts.post_title: Which specific test is used to demonstrate t…
posts.post_content: Which specific test is used to demonstrate the capsule of Bacillus anthracis for diagnostic confirmation of anthrax?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: McFadyen's reaction

McFadyen's reaction, using methylene blue staining, is used to demonstrate the capsule of Bacillus anthracis for diagnostic confirmation.

Correct Option Explanation

The Ascoli precipitation test can also confirm anthrax even from decomposed material by detecting a thermostable antigen, giving a white precipitate.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Coggins test is wrong — this AGID test detects antibodies in Equine Infectious Anaemia, not anthrax.
  • Straus test is wrong — this guinea pig inoculation test is used for Glanders diagnosis, not anthrax.
  • Habel's test is wrong — this mouse inoculation test is used for rabies diagnosis, not anthrax.
Know More
  • Anthrax spores form only after the carcass is opened.
  • Sheep and cattle are the most susceptible species.
  • Postmortem examination of suspected anthrax carcasses is generally avoided.
  • Human cutaneous anthrax is called 'Malignant Carbuncle'.

posts.post_title: Perosis (slipped tendon/chondrodystrophy) in…
posts.post_content: Perosis (slipped tendon/chondrodystrophy) in young birds can result from combined deficiency of which micronutrients?

_aimcq_options.text: Vitamin A and vitamin D only

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Manganese, zinc, choline and biotin

Perosis in young birds can result from combined deficiencies of manganese, zinc, choline and biotin, causing short, thick, misshapen long bones.

Correct Option Explanation

This multi-nutrient aetiology distinguishes perosis from single-vitamin deficiency syndromes like curled toe paralysis (riboflavin) or star gazing attitude (thiamine).

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Vitamin A and D only is wrong — these vitamins cause distinct deficiency syndromes (epithelial metaplasia, rickets), not the specific perosis combination.
  • Iron and copper only is wrong — these minerals are linked to anaemia syndromes, not perosis.
  • Sodium and chloride only is wrong — these electrolytes cause dehydration/salt-poisoning syndromes, unrelated to perosis.
Know More
  • Manganese is essential for cartilage matrix synthesis.
  • The gastrocnemius tendon slips from its normal position in affected birds.
  • Egg shell quality can also be affected by manganese deficiency in layers.
  • Niacin deficiency is also linked to a similar chondrodystrophy pattern in young birds.

posts.post_title: Which of the following best describes the pa…
posts.post_content: Which of the following best describes the pathogenesis-defining feature distinguishing 'Wet' from 'Dry' forms of Feline Infectious Peritonitis?

_aimcq_options.text: Presence versus absence of excessive fibrinous peritoneal/pleural effusion
Presence versus absence of any granulomas
Wet form is caused by a different virus entirely
Dry form is always fatal within days, wet form is chronic

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Presence versus absence of excessive fibrinous peritoneal/pleural effusion

The wet (effusive) form of FIP is distinguished by excessive fibrinous fluid accumulation in body cavities, while the dry (non-effusive) form lacks this significant effusion.

Correct Option Explanation

Both forms share the same coronavirus aetiology and underlying immune-complex-mediated vasculitis, differing mainly in the degree of vascular permeability and exudation.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Absence of granulomas is wrong — both wet and dry forms can show pyogranulomatous lesions; the key distinguishing feature is the presence of effusion.
  • Different virus entirely is wrong — both forms are caused by the same feline coronavirus, not different viruses.
  • Dry form always fatal within days is wrong — the disease's course length is not the primary distinguishing feature; effusion presence/absence is.
Know More
  • FIP has a slowly progressive course of one to several months.
  • Fluid accumulation in the wet form can reach up to 1 litre.
  • Multiple necrotic foci occur in liver, spleen and kidney in both forms.
  • The organism is antigenically related to canine coronavirus.

posts.post_title: Which mineral, when in excess relative to zi…
posts.post_content: Which mineral, when in excess relative to zinc, contributes to parakeratosis in pigs by forming insoluble complexes with zinc in the gut?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Calcium (and phosphorus)

Excess calcium (and phosphorus) in the diet interferes with zinc absorption by forming insoluble complexes, precipitating parakeratosis in pigs.

Correct Option Explanation

Phytic acid similarly binds zinc, reducing its bioavailability; both factors together commonly precipitate this skin condition in pig-rearing systems using mineral-supplemented diets.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Iron is wrong — iron is not the mineral described as antagonising zinc absorption in this context; calcium/phosphorus are.
  • Magnesium is wrong — magnesium deficiency causes tetany syndromes, and it is not the described zinc antagonist here.
  • Potassium is wrong — potassium is not implicated in zinc-binding or parakeratosis in this text.
Know More
  • Lesions include circumscribed erythematous areas of the abdomen and thighs.
  • Cattle show parakeratosis and alopecia similarly with zinc deficiency.
  • Sheep show wool loss with thick, wrinkled, crusted skin.
  • Poultry show poor feathering and scaly skin on legs and feet with zinc deficiency.

posts.post_title: Which of the following diseases is character…
posts.post_content: Which of the following diseases is characterized by intranuclear inclusion bodies in hepatocytes and vascular endothelium, along with a thickened, oedematous gall bladder?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Infectious Canine Hepatitis

Infectious Canine Hepatitis (caused by Canine Adenovirus I) shows intranuclear inclusion bodies in hepatocytes and endothelium along with a characteristic thickened, oedematous gall bladder.

Correct Option Explanation

This is a distinguishing gross feature from other canine viral diseases, alongside 'Blue eye syndrome' (corneal opacity) from immune complex deposition.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Canine Distemper is wrong — this paramyxoviral disease shows different inclusion patterns and a 'nutmeg liver' pattern, not the gall bladder change of ICH.
  • Canine Parvoviral Infection is wrong — this disease targets rapidly dividing cells (intestinal crypts, myocardium in pups), not hepatic intranuclear inclusions with gall bladder change.
  • Leptospirosis is wrong — this bacterial spirochaetal disease causes nephritis/jaundice, not the specific viral inclusion body pattern of ICH.
Know More
  • ICH was fully described by Rubarth in 1947.
  • Severe hypoglycaemia occurs due to hepatic injury.
  • The causative agent is Canine Adenovirus I, a DNA virus.
  • The disease is also known as Rubarth's disease.

posts.post_title: Which viral disease is characterized pathogn…
posts.post_content: Which viral disease is characterized pathognomonically by 'Negri bodies', round eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions with basophilic inner granules, found mainly in the hippocampus and cerebellar Purkinje cells?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Rabies

Negri bodies are pathognomonic round, eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions of Rabies, found especially in hippocampal and cerebellar Purkinje neurons.

Correct Option Explanation

These inclusions contain viral nucleoprotein and are a key histopathological diagnostic feature, along with microglial nodules called Babes nodules.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Canine Distemper is wrong — this disease shows both intranuclear and intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies, not specifically Negri bodies.
  • Aujeszky's Disease is wrong — this shows intranuclear inclusion bodies in degenerated neurons, not Negri bodies.
  • Infectious Canine Hepatitis is wrong — this shows intranuclear inclusions in hepatocytes and endothelium, not Negri bodies in neurons.
Know More
  • Rabies virus is a Rhabdovirus.
  • 'Fixed virus' from rabbit passage lacks Negri bodies, unlike 'street virus'.
  • Transmission is mainly via the bite of a rabid animal.
  • Cats show only the furious form of rabies; rabbits show only the dumb form.

posts.post_title: Which vitamin's deficiency is specifically t…
posts.post_content: Which vitamin's deficiency is specifically termed the 'anti-sterility factor' deficiency, given its role in reproduction and its close functional relationship with selenium?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Vitamin E

Vitamin E is known as the 'anti-sterility factor', and selenium is described as the 'Vitamin E sparer' due to their closely linked antioxidant roles.

Correct Option Explanation

Deficiency causes reproductive failure (e.g., fetal death in rats) as well as White Muscle Disease in calves/lambs and encephalomalacia in poultry.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Vitamin A is wrong — this vitamin's deficiency causes epithelial keratinisation and night blindness, and vitamin E is instead termed the 'vitamin A sparer'.
  • Vitamin D is wrong — this vitamin's deficiency causes rickets/osteomalacia, unrelated to the 'anti-sterility factor' designation.
  • Vitamin K is wrong — this vitamin's deficiency causes a haemorrhagic syndrome, not a reproductive/anti-sterility syndrome.
Know More
  • Alpha, beta and gamma tocopherols are the active forms of vitamin E.
  • Sources include germs of grains, green plants and oil seeds.
  • Vitamin E protects cell membranes from oxidative damage.
  • Deficiency in minks and pigs causes 'yellow fat disease' (steatitis).

posts.post_title: Which disease shows the pathognomonic findin…
posts.post_content: Which disease shows the pathognomonic finding of 'button ulcers' resulting from vascular infarction of the intestinal mucosa due to endothelial swelling in small arterioles?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Swine Fever

Swine Fever shows pathognomonic 'button ulcers' in the caecum and colon, resulting from infarction due to vascular occlusion by swollen, hydropic endothelial cells.

Correct Option Explanation

This vascular pathogenesis distinguishes Swine Fever's intestinal lesions from the mucosal ulceration seen in Rinderpest or PPR, which arise from direct lymphoid/epithelial necrosis.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • PPR is wrong — this disease shows diphtheritic plaques and 'zebra stripes', not button ulcers from vascular infarction.
  • Rinderpest is wrong — this disease shows 'zebra marking' haemorrhages, a different pathogenetic mechanism from Swine Fever's vascular infarcts.
  • TGE is wrong — this coronaviral disease causes villous atrophy of the small intestine, not colonic button ulcers from vascular infarction.
Know More
  • Swine Fever is caused by a Pestivirus.
  • Kidney shows a 'Turkey egg' appearance from subcapsular petechiae.
  • The pig is the only domestic animal naturally infected.
  • First recognised in 1885 in the United States.

posts.post_title: A calf presenting with severe stiffness ('wo…
posts.post_content: A calf presenting with severe stiffness ('wooden horse' gait in adults), hyperirritability and spastic paralysis following a deep puncture wound is most likely suffering from which disease?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Tetanus

Tetanus, caused by Clostridium tetani entering through deep wounds, produces hyperirritability and spastic paralysis due to tetanospasmin blocking inhibitory neurotransmission.

Correct Option Explanation

Horses and mules are highly susceptible, showing a classic stiff, 'wooden horse' gait as the toxin causes uncontrolled muscle contraction.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Botulism is wrong — this causes flaccid, not spastic, paralysis from blockade of acetylcholine release, the opposite clinical pattern.
  • Black Quarter is wrong — this causes necrotising myositis with gas and rancid odour, not the neurotoxic spastic paralysis of tetanus.
  • Rabies is wrong — while rabies causes CNS signs, it is transmitted by bite/saliva contact, not classically linked to deep puncture wound infection with spasticity.
Know More
  • Tetanus spores have a characteristic 'drum stick' shape.
  • No characteristic gross lesion is seen at necropsy; death is due to toxaemia.
  • The toxin binds to a substance called 'protagon' at inhibitory synapses.
  • Prevention includes tetanus antitoxin administration after wounding.

posts.post_title: Which disease is characterized by the pathog…
posts.post_content: Which disease is characterized by the pathognomonic finding of hepatic 'Koch's blue bodies' together with abomasal punched-out ulcers, distinguishing it from Babesiosis?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Theileriosis

Theileriosis is characterized by Koch's blue bodies (schizonts) in lymphocytes/monocytes along with abomasal punched-out ulcers, distinguishing it from Babesiosis.

Correct Option Explanation

In contrast, Babesiosis shows intraerythrocytic pear-shaped parasites without the lymphoid schizont stage or the characteristic abomasal ulceration.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Anaplasmosis is wrong — this disease shows a coccoid intraerythrocytic form without Koch's blue bodies or the abomasal ulcer pattern.
  • Babesiosis is wrong — this disease shows pear-shaped intraerythrocytic parasites, not Koch's blue bodies in lymphocytes.
  • Trypanosomiasis is wrong — this disease shows extracellular flagellates in plasma, not intracellular schizonts or abomasal ulcers.
Know More
  • T. annulata is the Theileria species reported in India.
  • Cytotoxic CD8+ cells kill infected lymphoblasts in immune survivors.
  • Diagnosis includes blood smear examination for the schizont stage.
  • High fever and lymph node swelling are prominent clinical signs.

posts.post_title: A dog presenting with painless, rhomboid ('d…
posts.post_content: A dog presenting with painless, rhomboid ('diamond skin') erythematous skin lesions after recent contact with pigs might suggest zoonotic transmission of which organism, primarily a swine pathogen?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae

Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae, the cause of Swine Erysipelas with its classic 'diamond skin' lesions, can cause zoonotic infection in humans known as 'Erysipeloid'.

Correct Option Explanation

The organism's toxin injures vessel walls causing the characteristic rhomboid erythema, and it can also cause chronic vegetative endocarditis in pigs.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Actinobacillus lignieresi is wrong — this organism causes wooden tongue disease, unrelated to diamond skin lesions or swine origin.
  • Corynebacterium pseudotuberculosis is wrong — this organism causes caseous lymphadenitis in sheep/goats, with an onion-ring abscess pattern, not diamond skin lesions.
  • Mycoplasma mycoides is wrong — this organism causes Contagious Bovine Pleuropneumonia, a respiratory disease unrelated to diamond skin lesions.
Know More
  • Erysipelothrix also affects sheep, cattle and birds.
  • Young pigs aged 3–6 months are most susceptible to erysipelas.
  • Chronic form shows vegetative valvular endocarditis, typically of the mitral valve.
  • Human erysipeloid is typically an occupational infection in those handling pork or fish.

posts.post_title: Which classic finding on liver histopatholog…
posts.post_content: Which classic finding on liver histopathology — fibrosis and calcification of bile ducts producing a rigid, protruding duct on cut section — is seen in chronic infection by which parasite?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Fasciola hepatica/gigantica

Chronic Fasciola hepatica/gigantica infection produces fibrosis and calcification of bile ducts, giving the classic 'pipe stem' or 'clay pipe' liver appearance.

Correct Option Explanation

This results from long-standing cholangiohepatitis and biliary epithelial hyperplasia caused by the irritant presence of adult flukes within the bile ducts.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Ascaris suum is wrong — this roundworm causes 'milk spot' liver lesions from larval migration tracks, not bile duct calcification.
  • Echinococcus granulosus is wrong — this tapeworm larva forms discrete hydatid cysts, not diffuse bile duct fibrosis/calcification.
  • Moniezia expansa is wrong — this intestinal tapeworm of ruminants does not cause hepatic bile duct lesions at all.
Know More
  • The intermediate host of Fasciola is the snail Lymnaea.
  • Fascioloides magna wanders in the peritoneal cavity before invading the liver.
  • Chronic disease presents with anaemia and submandibular oedema.
  • Ova are oval, pedunculated and golden brown.
